# Knight of Lodis Recomp: development log

The working notes of the project, kept in order as the work went: every
feature, fix, measurement and failed approach, with the switches to try them.
The project's overview is the [README](../README.md). Code comments that
cite a README section (README "...") mean a section of this file.


A static recompilation project for **Tactics Ogre: The Knight of Lodis**
(Game Boy Advance, USA release, game code `ATOE`), built on
[GBARecomp](https://github.com/mstan/gbarecomp).

This is an experimental preservation / research project, not a finished
port. It does not include or distribute the game ROM, the GBA BIOS, or any
extracted game assets. You need your own legally obtained copy of the
cartridge dump to build or run anything here.

## Status (2026-09-17)

This project has a **running, statically-recompiled executable** that
boots the real game through the recompiled BIOS and recompiled cartridge
code via `runtime_dispatch`, with cart-ROM coverage fully static and a
real hardware-oracle diffing loop now running against it (see below —
it already found and fixed one genuine bug in the shared framework). It
is not accurate or complete yet; treat everything below as exactly what
it says and nothing more.

- [x] ROM identity verified: SHA-1 `85a46320a31f16f5c6dda27fc094edd078dbe43d`,
      MD5 `5d4f385e4e1cfa4a057d0ac828993906`, 8 MiB, entry point
      `0x080000C0` (standard header, nothing exotic). Save chip
      auto-detected from the ROM signature as **Flash 64KB (512 Kbit,
      `FLASH_V` signature)**.
- [x] Static function discovery (`gba_recompile --rom totkol.gba --config
      game.toml`): 38,215 functions, all but 12 found with **zero manual
      seeds**. The 12 hand-added `[[extra_func]]` entries plus 6
      `[[resume_range]]` entries in `game.toml` are documented there with
      the miss evidence and disassembly that justified each one. Every
      generated shard compiles and links cleanly.
- [x] `src/main.cpp` + `CMakeLists.txt` wire the generated cart dispatch
      table into `gbarecomp::run_game()` (the shared runtime's real
      per-game entry point — see `gbarecomp/src/runtime/runtime.h`). The
      project builds by adding the sibling `gbarecomp` checkout as a
      CMake subdirectory and linking `gbarecomp_runtime` via its
      `target_link_gbarecomp_runtime_stack()` helper.
- [x] **Verified boot, headless, cold self-heal cache, up to 9000 frames
      (~150 s of game time):** `dispatch_misses` is down to exactly 4,
      all four IWRAM (RAM) addresses, with **zero** cart-ROM code misses
      of any kind. Screenshots pulled via `--dump-bmp` at increasing
      frame counts show, in order: the "Licensed by Nintendo" splash
      (~frame 300) and legible, continuing story-intro narration and art
      through frame 5000 — i.e. this is genuinely running the game, not
      spinning on a black screen.
- [x] **Interior-entry-point cluster closed — it was never a jump table.**
      Disassembled the `0x0815BC80`–`0x0815BDB0` region directly with
      gbarecomp's own ARM/Thumb decoder (a throwaway standalone tool
      linked against `libgbarecomp_armv4t.a`) instead of guessing from
      the miss log. It's a run of tiny MP2K-style trampoline functions
      (`mov r12,lr / bl <shared helper> / store / bx r12`); the runtime's
      own `jump_table_candidate` flag on some of these PCs was a false
      positive from its "misses are close together" heuristic. Fixed
      with 10 `[[extra_func]]` entries for the trampoline entries
      themselves plus one `[[resume_range]]` covering every interior
      call-return point in the whole region — the right tool, since which
      exact interior PC gets hit shifts with self-heal cache timing (one
      new sibling point appeared on a fresh run after the first fix and
      the range covers it automatically). The same disassembly-first
      method found four *earlier* individual `[[extra_func]]` entries
      from an earlier round were actually misclassified the same way and
      converted those to `[[resume_range]]` entries too — see `game.toml`
      for the full reasoning and exact addresses.
- [x] **The `0x08000000` hit is understood and fixed — it was never a
      header/data risk.** Disassembled it directly: address `0x08000000`
      holds a genuine, valid `b 0x080000C0` instruction, not header data.
      An earlier revision of this file mischaracterized it as "inside the
      title/checksum bytes" — wrong; the real GBA header layout puts the
      entry branch at bytes 0x00-0x03 and the logo/title/checksum well
      after it. `0x08000000` is the actual hardware GBA boot entry point
      every real console jumps to; it just branches past the
      non-executable header data to the code at `entry_pc`. Our discovery
      walk starts one hop downstream at `entry_pc` (`0x080000C0`) as an
      optimization, so nothing in the reachable graph pointed back at the
      redundant first hop — except the recompiled BIOS's own
      hardware-accurate boot sequence, once. Fixed with a single
      `[[extra_func]]` entry; see `game.toml` for the full writeup.
- [ ] One item remains, not blocking: a few IWRAM (RAM, `0x03xxxxxx`)
      addresses the interpreter still bridges. This is correct, expected
      behavior, not a bug: RAM-resident code isn't part of the ROM image
      `gba_recompile` reads, so it can never get a static `game.toml`
      entry — it's the shared runtime's RAM self-heal tier's job
      (`g_runtime_ram_dispatch_hook`), and right now those particular
      hits fail to compile to native and stay interpreted (`failed=4` in
      the exit banner). Not investigated.
- [x] **Sound engine identified as MP2K/Sappy.** A one-time diagnostic
      dump (`hang_dump.log`, not committed) captured the M4A sound-mixer
      state mid-run with 6 active channels, confirming this game drives
      the standard GBA MP2K audio engine that `gbarecomp/src/gba/gba_m4a.*`
      and `mp2k_shadow.cpp` already model.
- [x] **The "hang" is a watchdog false positive, not a game bug — resolved.**
      A headless run tripped the runtime's built-in hang watchdog
      (`src/runtime/runtime_bus_bridge.cpp`, "guest has not HALTed for
      several seconds"). Re-tested directly: it reproduces on repeat
      headless `--frames 2000` runs, cold *and warm* self-heal cache, at
      a *different* PC each time (`0x0815D014` the first time,
      `0x080013C2` the next) — a real bug would localize to one PC, a
      generic timing heuristic wouldn't. Both runs completed normally
      afterward (exit 0, no corruption, no stuck process): the watchdog
      fires once, dumps a diagnostic snapshot (`hang_dump.log` /
      `hang_trace.csv`, gitignored), and keeps going — it's explicitly
      "observation, not a fix" per its own source comment, not a game
      halt. The name is also misleading out of context: `MC-HP-002` is
      an unrelated, already-known bug specific to *The Minish Cap*'s
      sound engine; the watchdog message just reuses that label as a
      generic "this shape of symptom" tag, not a claim that this game
      has that bug. Root cause: the watchdog is a 4-second *wall-clock*
      timer (`GBARECOMP_HANG_SECONDS`, default 4), and a headless run
      fast-forwards through self-heal recompilation of the still-open
      `0x0815B8xx` cluster fast enough, in real time, to occasionally
      outrun that fixed threshold even though the guest is fine. It's
      cosmetic for headless batch testing; disable with
      `GBARECOMP_HANG_WATCHDOG=0` if the log noise gets in the way.
      **Sharper answer, 2026-09-21:** it is not a timing accident at all for
      this game. KoL's mainline is an empty task loop that never executes a
      HALT — every frame of work happens in the VBlank handler — so the
      watchdog's one and only signal is absent by construction, and it trips
      on any run long enough in wall-clock terms, including a cold boot that
      reaches the title screen and exits 0. Treat a trip here as noise, and
      see the "Return to Title Screen" section below for what it cost.
- [x] **Oracle diffing against mGBA is set up and running** — see the
      "Real hardware verification" section below. OAM/PAL/VRAM/EWRAM are
      byte-identical to a real GBA core across the tested window.
- [x] **Menu navigation and a save/load round-trip are confirmed**
      (2026-09-21, on the Thor): saving writes a 64 KB `totkol.sav`, and
      after a force-stop and cold boot the title menu's CONTINUE ->
      "Continue from save" restores the world map. This needed two
      framework fixes first — see "Saving failed, and the save never
      reached disk" below. New-game from start to finish is still
      unexercised.

Read that literally: booting into the license screen and story intro is a
real milestone, and it is also very far from "this game runs correctly."
Both statements are true at once and this file will not blur them.

## Saving failed, and the save never reached disk — SOLVED 2026-09-21

Two separate bugs, both in the framework, both found from one report (saving
the game failed). `states/AH_save_screen.state` is the repro — the save screen
with three NO DATA slots; press A and the old build says **"Failed to save
data"**.

**1. The flash chip reported the wrong device ID.** The model answered the
autoselect query with maker `0xC2`, device `0x09` — a Macronix MX29L010, a
**1 Mbit** part — for every cartridge, under a comment claiming the 512 Kbit
drivers accept it too. They do not. This cart is `FLASH_V`, a 512 Kbit part.

The game's driver reads the ident at ROM `0x08158F24`:

```
0x08158F32  strb 0xAA -> 0x0E005555      ; unlock
0x08158F3C  strb 0x55 -> 0x0E002AAA
0x08158F40  strb 0x90 -> 0x0E005555      ; autoselect
            ... delay loop ...
0x08158F66  bl <veneer `bx r5`>          ; r5 = sp|1 -- reads 0x0E000001
0x08158F72  bl <veneer `bx r5`>          ;              reads 0x0E000000
            r4 = (device << 8) | maker
0x08158F8A  strb 0xF0 -> 0x0E005555      ; leave autoselect
```

**The read runs from a routine the game copies onto its own stack**, which is
why `GBARECOMP_READ_WATCH` never sees it — that is the interpreted
`0x03007E5C` in the boot banner, not a bus read from generated code. It cost
an hour of "the game never reads the chip".

The ident selects a `FlashType` descriptor, whose pointer is stored at EWRAM
`0x02029C18`. With `0x09C2` the identify function failed, and AgbMain then
**cleared that pointer** at `0x080003DA` — the "no save chip" state. From then
on every save failed without one command reaching the chip.

The device ID now follows the size: `0x1C` (MX29L512) at 64 KB, `0x09`
(MX29L010) at 128 KB. Loading a savestate re-derives it too, rather than
trusting the blob — the chip is a property of the ROM, which the snapshot
already gates on by SHA-1, and every state written before the fix carries the
wrong device into a fixed build otherwise.

Measured at each step: the guest now reads `0x1C`/`0xC2`, the probe selects
descriptor `0x0824DE64` whose ident at `+0x14` is the `0x1CC2` the driver's
check at `0x08159200` demands, and the clear of `0x02029C18` no longer
happens.

**2. The save never reached disk on Android.** With the ID fixed the game
saved — the slot went from NO DATA to "Lv. 2 Alphonse / Solea / Vento 5" — and
`files/totkol.sav` was still not created. The battery auto-flush lived only at
the bottom of the runner's outer loop, and **under present-in-place a windowed
session can stay inside one `step_once()` for its whole life**, so that loop
may never come round again. The save sat in RAM, and a force-stop threw it
away. The flush is now called from the present hook as well.

**That is the same shape as the title-return freeze above** — work parked at
the runner's dispatch boundary does not happen when the guest never returns
there. Anything else still living only in that loop is worth a look.

**This closes "Next steps" item 1**, the save/load round-trip that had never
been reachable. On the Thor: saving writes a 64 KB `totkol.sav` with 8164
bytes programmed (the same count as desktop), and after a force-stop and cold
boot the title menu offers CONTINUE, "Continue from save" is enabled, and
loading lands back on the world map at Solea with 3500 Goth.

**One trap for anyone re-testing this.** A savestate taken before the fix
cannot validate it: it carries the stale chip identity in the blob *and* the
guest's own cleared `0x02029C18` in EWRAM, so pressing A still fails. Only a
fresh boot re-probes. `states/AH_save_screen_patched.state` is that state with
the one pointer hand-poked to `0x0824DE64` — a test fixture, not a fix, and
the only way to exercise the erase/program path without playing to a save
point.

## "Return to Title Screen" froze the picture — SOLVED 2026-09-21

The world map's CHECK prompt -> Yes stopped the device on a half-faded map
forever: no abort, no crash, the process alive. It reproduces on desktop from
`states/AG_title_return.state` with `GBARECOMP_INPUT_REPLAY` pressing A.

**It was never the guest that froze.** The game was running the whole time.
What stopped was the RUNNER: over the TCP rig (`--tcp`, then `continue`, which
keeps the debug server answering while the core is wedged) the `frame` command
— the runner's completed-frame counter — sat at 1060864 while `run_status`
reported `ppu.frame_count()` climbing past 1064242 and 3397 vblanks. The guest
was still taking interrupts, still writing IE, still advancing its scene task's
state machine. Nothing was being presented.

**Root cause: the game soft-resets from inside its VBlank handler.** Every
frame of KoL's real work runs in the handler at ROM `0x080005A0`; the mainline
at `0x0800056E` is an empty task loop. "Return to Title Screen" branches from
that handler straight to `0x080000C0` — the cartridge entry point, the crt0
that does `msr cpsr,#0x12; ldr sp,...; msr cpsr,#0x1F; ldr sp,...` and then
calls AgbMain. It never performs an exception return. On hardware that is free.
In the recomp `runtime_irq()` is a real host C frame whose drive-to-completion
loop waits for exactly that iret, so `g_irq_nest_depth` stuck at 1 and
`runtime_should_yield()` refused every VBlank yield from then on.

Fixed in gbarecomp (`ae56c3c`): `runtime_should_yield()` recognises a branch to
the machine's restart entry while a handler is live, parks the PC, and unwinds
the whole generated chain to the runner, which resumes there. The entry is
decoded from the ROM header's own branch, not hard-coded. Pressing A now
reboots the game, plays the opening and lands on the title screen — confirmed
on desktop and on the Thor.

**Two things worth not re-learning.**

1. **The hang watchdog is a FALSE POSITIVE on this game, and it cost a
   session.** It fires on "the guest has not HALTed for several seconds", and
   KoL never HALTs: its main loop busy-spins while the VBlank handler does the
   work. A plain cold boot that reaches the title screen and exits 0 trips it
   too. `hang_trace.csv` then contains 4096 records of that idle loop
   (`0x08000584..0x080008C8`), which reads exactly like a freeze and is not
   one. The previous session took the trip and the trace as the diagnosis and
   spent itself chasing a spin that was the game's ordinary idle.
2. **`--frames N` cannot terminate a run whose frame boundary never comes**, so
   "headless hangs" and "guest hangs" look identical from the outside. Compare
   the runner's frame counter against the PPU's before concluding anything.

## Widened margins outrun the guest's tilemap streaming — SOLVED 2026-09-20

**Read "The composed map is in EWRAM" below first: the margins no longer come
from the guest's tilemap at all, and none of the trade-offs weighed here apply
any more.** The section is kept because the measurement in it is what located
the real source, and because the two rejected fixes are worth not re-trying.

Reported as the right edge of the screen being mangled, and sometimes the
left. Reproduced on `states/U_edge_mangle.state` at width 320.

The guest writes its tilemap **just in time** for a 240-wide view, keeping only
a narrow border beyond it. A 320-wide view needs about five more tile columns
per side than the guest guarantees to have written, so margin samples hit cells
that are still empty and fall through to the backdrop — a sky-coloured wedge.
It appears on whichever side the camera last moved away from, which is why it
swaps sides.

Measured with `KOL_COVERAGE=<width>`, which reports pixels no regular BG layer
draws at all (not a colour guess):

| view | left margin bare | right margin bare |
|------|------------------|-------------------|
| 256  | 0.0%             | 23.4%             |
| 284  | 0.0%             | 34.3%             |
| 320  | 0.8%             | **45.9%**         |

The authentic 240 frame is itself 3.3% bare, so the guest shows backdrop past
its own map edge too; 320 simply shows much more of it.

**Two causes, in proportion.** Scrolling right refilled columns 55 and 56 (14
rows to 21 and 20), so roughly **28%** of the bare area is streaming lag the
guest would fill if the camera moved. The other **~72%** is the map's real
edge: the tile data ends on a diagonal staircase, which is why the boundary
looks ragged rather than like a border.

### Replaying remembered columns — tried, measured, reverted

The obvious fix was to reuse the shadow built for the see-through highlight:
remember each tilemap cell while it is populated and replay it when the guest
has not written it yet, with the same ring-recycle invalidation so a slot
standing for a different world column is never replayed.

It was implemented and it works as designed — the provider fired 3.5M times
and substituted 2.7M entries. It also recovers **nothing you can see**.
Instrumented per frame, the number of cells that are empty on screen AND have a
remembered entry was **0 almost always, peaking at 2** across a 260-frame scroll
out and back, against 2935 bare pixels in that margin. Rendered output with the
replay on and off was **byte-identical**.

The reason is structural, and worth keeping: the guest writes a column just
before it needs to display it, and the recycle rule correctly drops a cell the
moment its slot starts standing for a different world column. Together those
mean a cell that is empty *and on screen* has essentially never been seen
populated for the world column the camera is asking about — the guest has not
got there yet. A shadow can only replay ground already covered, and by the time
it is covered the guest has written it, so there is nothing left to replay.

Reverted rather than shipped: it cost a per-pixel callback across every margin
sample and bought about two tile cells, once. `KOL_COVERAGE` is kept, since it
is what turned this from an argument into a measurement.

### Masking the margin was measured, and every version made it worse

Before the EWRAM map was found, the only lever appeared to be *which margin
columns to draw*. Measured with `KOL_MARGIN_TRACE=1` (added to
`src/kol_terrain_probe.cpp`), which reports per frame how many tile columns
past its own window the guest has populated:

- while the camera MOVES, the guest keeps **two** tile columns (16 px) on the
  side it is moving toward, never four or five;
- the **third** column — 16..24 px out — flips populated/empty with every 8 px
  of scroll (35 flips on the left over a 190-step zigzag);
- columns four and five are simply never written until the camera catches up;
- the trailing side meanwhile holds up to 15 columns.

At 320 the margin is five tile columns, so the outer three are exactly the ones
that appear and vanish. **A margin sample can only be dropped, never invented**
— suppressing a column and drawing an unwritten one both leave the backdrop —
so masking cannot fill the gap, it can only hide the flicker by never drawing
those columns at all. Simulated against the recorded traces (1,199 frames, 190
camera steps, 19 direction reversals), counting visible appear/disappear
events and the mean number of the 10 margin columns drawn:

| policy | events | mean columns drawn |
|---|---|---|
| draw everything (then-current) | 83 | 8.22 |
| fixed 16 px content limit per side | **0** | 4.00 |
| limit the LEADING side only | 118 | 7.06 |
| limit both sides while the camera moves | 171 | 5.18 |

Only a permanent clip removes the flicker, and it costs half the widened
battlefield; every state-dependent rule *adds* events, because hiding and
revealing are themselves transitions. A 16 px clip was built and shown on the
device, and rejected there: the ask was a wider view that renders correctly,
not a narrower one that holds still.

## The composed map is in EWRAM, and the margins read it (2026-09-20)

**The guest composes the WHOLE map as tilemap entries in EWRAM and blits a
moving window of it into VRAM.** The VRAM tilemap is a lagging cache, not the
source. So the margins do not need the tilemap: they can read the entry the
guest itself would have written, which is exact, immediate, and available for
every column of the map at once.

Found by watching the guest rather than guessing at layouts:
`GBARECOMP_WRITE_WATCH=06006000,06008000` during a scroll gives the blit
(`strh` at `0x08025672`, BG0 and BG1 written by one routine), and
`GBARECOMP_READ_WATCH` on EWRAM gives what that store copies **from**.

```
array  = u32 at 0x02026CA8          BG0; BG1 is the same array + 0x6000
stride = 0x100 bytes = 128 u16 columns, 96 rows
entry  = array + row * 0x100 + col * 2, ordinary tilemap entries
```

**Where the camera is in that array cannot be read off BGxHOFS/VOFS.** The
tilemap is a 64x32 ring over a map up to 128x96, so `vofs / 8` is short by 32
rows wherever the camera has passed the wrap — five of twelve reference states
sit past it, and a vofs-derived row matches 2.5%-15% there. The wrap is
resolved instead by **matching the guest's own drawn cells**: try each
candidate ring, keep the one whose entries equal what is already on screen.
Last frame's answer is tried first, so the common frame costs one pass.

That makes the lookup self-checking, which is the property that matters —
drawing scenery the guest did not compose is the one thing this must never do.
`map_source_tick()` re-runs the check every frame over every drawn cell and
refuses to serve the margins when agreement drops below 95%, falling back to
the previous behaviour. Measured: **100% of drawn cells on all twelve
reference states, both layers**, and 100% on every frame of a 1,199-frame
zigzag scroll and of a session on the device.

A byte pair in the same struct (`(int8)[0x02026C94]+2`, `[0x02026C95]+2`) holds
the window origin at rest and matched all twelve states — and it is **not**
used, because it does not track the camera during a scroll (measured 23 rows
out mid-move). Positioning the lookup with it tore the margin by whole tiles on
60 frames of that same scroll. Position from the scroll register, disambiguate
with content.

**Result**, same zigzag, BG0, appear/disappear events per margin tile column:

| source | offset 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | mean columns with content |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| guest tilemap, left | 0 | 0 | 35 | 11 | 11 | 3.19 of 5 |
| guest tilemap, right | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 1 | 4.90 of 5 |
| composed map, both | **0** | **0** | **0** | **0** | **0** | **5.00 of 5** |

No measurable cost: 32.6 fps against 32.5 with `KOL_WS_NO_MAP_SOURCE=1`, same
state, 900 frames. Verified on the Thor at 320: margins carry map to both
edges, agreement 100%, no fallback while playing.

**The contiguity rule below is now a fallback, not the policy.** It exists to
reject stale ring content showing through where the tilemap had run out; the
composed map has no such content, so when the lookup is armed the rule is
skipped. State `E_water_tile_margin`, whose floating island it was written for,
renders **byte-identically** either way — the island is absent from the array,
which is why the heuristic agreed with it.

`KOL_WS_NO_MAP_SOURCE=1` reverts to the tilemap-and-contiguity behaviour for an
A/B; `KOL_MAP_SOURCE_STATS=1` reports agreement and the resolved wrap.


### A still camera keeps the margins (2026-09-25)

Toggling view mode in battle preparation made the margins flash for one
frame. On that frame the guest repaints the deployment highlight, and VRAM
and the composed array disagree on 13.2% of the drawn cells (86.8% of 622).
The camera does not move: same HOFS/VOFS, same ring, and 100% on the frames
either side. Below the 95% bar the source fell back, and the margins showed
the wrapped tilemap for that frame: a torn slab beside the info panel and
terrain in the bottom margin.

`map_source_tick()` now keeps serving, for at most 2 frames in a row, when
all of these hold:
- it was serving;
- the best ring is the one last served;
- both layers' scroll registers equal those last served;
- agreement is still at least 80%.

A wrong pointer, a rebuilt map, or anything with the camera moving fails
as before. Repro: `states/BD_units_invisible.state` at 480x270, with L as
in "Flashes on view mode". Before, it logged "falling back after 40 frames
serving" and "…after 106"; now it logs no fallback.

**The 80% floor was too high (lowered to 25% on 2026-09-26).** Selecting a
unit repaints the whole move range a frame before the array follows, and
agreement fell to 51.7% on select and 67.9% on cancel, with the camera still.
At 80% each fell back for one frame, and the wrapped tilemap put the top of
the map in the bottom margin, reported as a flash of terrain on select and
cancel (`states/BR_flash_on_select.state`, 480x270: A on Alphonse, then B,
B). A repaint cannot move the map; only the camera can, and a moving camera
is already excluded. 25% still refuses a different scene, and the 2-frame
bound still holds. Verified on desktop and on the Thor, where the log shows
no fallback on either press. Both invariants unchanged.

**And the camera a tile on (2026-10-17).** The user, on states/HQ (the
burning town, map 99, the camera panning), reported the sky flickering in
the widescreen margins on the fire scene. Twice in 40 frames the margins went for a
frame and the backdrop's sky stood around the native picture (warped by
the perspective, a trapezoid of town in the sky). Both were frames where
the scroll had just crossed into the next tile (registers 28,44 -> 27,45,
then 27,45 -> 27,46): 85.2% and 82.8% of the drawn cells agreed, the
frame after 100%. The guest's tilemap is behind its scroll for that frame;
the array is right. So a moving camera may serve too, when the ring is the
one last served, each layer's registers moved at most a tile, at least
half the drawn cells agree, at most 2 frames in a row; served at the new
registers. `KOL_MAP_SOURCE_NO_STEP_GRACE=1`: falls back, as before. HQ now
serves the whole fire scene (170 frames) and no frame has the sky jump;
AS, BR, GH and HN are byte-identical over 400 presents at 480x270; both
invariants hold.

## Absolute frame counts — a trap this project has now hit three times

`ExtendedViewFrameInfo`'s frame number, and `ppu.frame_count()`, are the
**absolute** PPU frame count. A save state carries its own count over, so a
state saved deep into a session resumes at, say, frame 97606, not 0. Any
diagnostic that gates on a frame number therefore has to count RELATIVE to the
start of the run, and has to latch its origin somewhere that actually runs after
the state is applied.

Three separate pieces of tooling have been caught by this:

1. `GBARECOMP_INPUT_REPLAY` takes absolute frames, so a replay authored against
   one run silently did nothing against another (the load frame differed, 49303
   vs 44354).
2. `KOL_BG_DUMP_AT` first gated on the absolute count, so "dump at frame 45"
   fired immediately. That produced an apparent 104-cell tilemap difference that
   sent the base-map hunt down a blind alley — see the section above.
3. `KOL_DRIVE_SELECT`'s script latched its origin on the first probe tick, which
   happens BEFORE the state is applied, with `frame == 0`. The state then jumped
   the counter to 97606 and every scripted keypress sat ~97000 frames in the
   past. The fixed-cycle driver survived only because it used `rel % 120`, which
   still cycles no matter what the offset is — so the bug hid behind a working
   sibling.

The rule: latch the origin on the first frame where the scene you care about is
actually live (`is_battle_scene()`), not on the first call. `maybe_snap_map` and
`maybe_dump_bg` get this right only because they return early until the battle
map is up, which is accidental rather than deliberate — do it on purpose.


## Map mirror at 0x02008440 — and why it is NOT a base map

**Corrected 2026-09-18.** An earlier version of this section claimed this array
was the pre-highlight base map and called the hunt solved. That was wrong. The
claim is kept here, corrected, rather than deleted, because the way it went
wrong is the useful part.

### What is actually true

`0x02008440` in EWRAM is a **mirror of the current BG0 tilemap**: row stride
`0x100` bytes (128 u16), 2 bytes per cell, full tilemap entries (tile index in
bits 0-9, palette bank in bits 12-15). The 32-row tilemap is a ring over a
taller world map, and rows past the wrap resolve at exactly **-32 rows**.

Verified on `states/T_move_highlight2.state`: with the wrap applied, **all 564
non-empty cells match, 100%, every row**. The address is the same in two
different battles, so it is not a per-battle allocation.

### What it does NOT do

It does not retain the pre-highlight tile. On `T`, for all 164 highlighted
cells, the mirror holds the **highlight** value and **zero** hold the original.
Re-running the same check properly on `S` gives the same answer: 104 of 104 hold
the highlight, none hold the original.

**The original tiles are in no guest memory at all while the highlight is
displayed** — searched exhaustively across EWRAM (256 KB), IWRAM (32 KB) and
VRAM (96 KB), for the full entry and for the tile index with the palette bank
stripped. No match anywhere. The game therefore *regenerates* the original tiles
when the highlight clears, from a more compact per-cell representation (terrain
type and height), rather than restoring them from a saved tilemap.

### How the wrong conclusion was reached

The first pass compared three files from **three different processes**: a
highlighted tilemap from one run, a cleared tilemap from a second, and an EWRAM
snapshot from a third. Cross-process comparison of a scrolling ring buffer is
not a controlled measurement, and the drive script was pressing B during frames
0-3, so samples meant to be "before" were already after the cancel. That produced
an apparent 100% match against the cleared map which no single-process run
reproduces.

The methodology that settles it, and the one to use next time: take **every
sample inside one process** (`KOL_MAP_SNAP="a,b"`), drive the input well after
the first snapshot, and check the specific cells known to have changed rather
than an aggregate match percentage. An aggregate hid this for hours — 91% "match"
was mostly cells that were never highlighted and so could not distinguish the
two hypotheses at all.

### Where that leaves a semi-transparent highlight

Recovering the original tile from memory is **ruled out**, not merely unfinished.
Two routes remain:

1. **Find the tile generator.** The game rebuilds the original tiles on cancel;
   that routine and its input map data would give the original for any cell at
   any time. This is a deeper hunt than the one attempted here — it means
   identifying an assembly routine, not finding an array.
2. **Shadow the tilemap.** Record each cell's entry while it is un-highlighted
   and blend against the remembered value. Needs no reverse-engineering and
   shares all of its rendering work with route 1, but a cell never observed
   un-highlighted — a cold save-state load into an active highlight, or newly
   scrolled-in terrain — has nothing to blend against and must fall back to the
   current opaque look. That fallback has to be visible in the design, not
   silent.

Either way an opt-in centre-of-screen compositing seam is required;
`g_ws_tilemap_provider` is margin-only, and this would deliberately change the
faithful render.

### Route 2, keyed on the world — done 2026-09-24

Route 2 shipped first keyed on VRAM RING slots, and that is why the range went
opaque while the map scrolled: a slot has to be dropped the moment it leaves
the window (it is recycled for different terrain), and a cell scrolled in under
an open range was never seen clean. At 270 lines the ring could not even name
the cell — 34 tile rows on screen against a 32-row ring.

The shadow is now kept per WORLD cell, filled from the composed map
(`kol_map_source`, whole battlefield in EWRAM). The highlight is painted into
that array too, so every cell is seen clean the first frame the battle is up,
long before a range opens or the camera reaches it. Measured on
`states/AV_pre_range.state` (the user's slot 2): the whole array, 2 x 96 x 128
= 24,576 cells, recorded on the first frame, none of them highlight-inked;
opening the range changed 138 cells and all 138 classified as highlight.

- **Placement.** A new optional seam, `g_ws_bg_underlay_sample_provider`
  (gbarecomp), passes the screen sample instead of the wrapped tile; KoL
  places it with `map_source_world_cell`, the margins' own mapping.
- **Cost of keeping it.** Each frame compares the array with last frame's copy
  a row at a time and classifies only cells that changed; the terrain never
  changes in a battle, so that is 192 row compares. AU at a real 480x270,
  three alternating runs: +0.04 ms/frame; with the range open +0.06 ms
  (7.07 -> 7.13), part of which is simply blending pixels that used to be drawn
  opaque.
- **Reset.** On every state load (`g_runtime_state_epoch`, bumped by every
  load path: `--load-state`, the BACK-menu slots, rewind) and on leaving the
  battle map.
- **Fallback, still, by design:** a state loaded INTO an open range stays
  opaque until the range is cancelled once. Only the tile generator
  (route 1) could fix that.

Verified: `KOL_HIGHLIGHT_WORLD_CHECK=1` compares ring and world shadows over
the authentic 240x160 wherever both exist — 356,866 cells agree, 0 differ,
0 where only the ring had one, across a scroll. After six Left presses the
old build draws the range as opaque slabs and the new one keeps it
see-through; every changed pixel was highlight blue.
`KOL_WS_NO_HIGHLIGHT_WORLD=1` and `KOL_WS_NO_MAP_SOURCE=1` each reproduce
the old build byte for byte. Both invariants unchanged (240 `66e13ab2`, 284
`84a95b05`, centre-240 0/160 rows).

**Driving it headlessly:** after A opens the range, the NAVI prompt "Choose
where you want to move this character." swallows the D-pad until a SECOND A
closes it. Directions before that do nothing at all (the frames are
byte-identical), which reads exactly like broken input injection.
`KOL_DRIVE_SELECT="10:A,120:A,200:L,212:L,224:L,236:L,248:L,260:L"`, dump at
290.

**Opaque after the unit sheets (2026-11-02).** The user, on states/thor/0104
(map 19, Clear Move Range on): A shows the range clear; opening the
character sheets with B, going back to battle with B and pressing A again
left the move range graphically broken. The range came up
as the game's own solid tiles, blue to white down the screen.
- The unit sheets are not the battle map, so the shadows are reset. Back on
  the map the array is read the first frame it is armed, but some terrain
  tiles still hold the window's art, which uses the highlight's index: 950
  terrain cells were taken for highlight and never recorded. A cell was
  read again only when its array entry changed, and here only the art had
  changed. A probe on row 100 under the open range: the reference had every
  cell's shadow, the broken run FFFF on six of eight.
- Now the cells read as inked are looked at again every frame by their
  tile's art as it is then: one whose art no longer holds the index is
  recorded, and its range mask (the lighting's and the water's) cleared.
  Before A is pressed every cell is clean again.
- Checked on 0104: B, B, A shows the range clear; A at once byte-identical
  to before; `KOL_HIGHLIGHT_NO_RECHECK=1` gives the broken picture byte for
  byte. The 52-render set: one change, 0039 (map 63, the night camp, no
  range): 15 px of shade near the tents, where 13 terrain cells use the
  index in their own art and had been spared from the lighting as range
  until their art changed. Both invariants hold.

## Why this looks the way it does

This project follows the workflow and ground rules of the parent
framework — see `../gbarecomp/CLAUDE.md`, `PRINCIPLES.md`, and `DEBUG.md`
for the actual rules (not restated here). In short:

- The GBA BIOS is recompiled and dispatched, never stubbed or HLE'd.
- A dispatch miss self-heals at runtime (interpret → recompile → cache)
  and is loudly logged — it never becomes a silent, permanent interpreter
  path.
- `game.toml` is hand-maintained. `gba_recompile` never writes to it;
  miss-log-derived proposals land in `recomp_seed_proposals.toml` and are
  merged in only after human review.
- `generated/` is 100% derived from the ROM you supply. It is gitignored,
  regenerated locally, and never hand-edited.

## Layout

```
KnightOfLodisRecomp/
  game.toml           hand-maintained per-binary recompile config
  src/main.cpp        the whole per-game entry point — see below
  CMakeLists.txt       pulls in ../gbarecomp via add_subdirectory
  symbols/             (future) imported/curated symbol tables
  generated/           gba_recompile output — gitignored, regenerate locally
  totkol.gba           your own ROM dump — gitignored, not included
  framework/, build/    local build scratch — gitignored
  shots/                local-only reference screenshots — gitignored
```

## Building and running

Requires a sibling checkout of
[`gbarecomp`](https://github.com/mstan/gbarecomp) (pinned at
`ed9824b70aa350cd9e1653894beaf6b1b6b27787` as of this writing, built once
per its own README so `../gbarecomp/build/gba_recompile` and the toml++
header exist) and your own `totkol.gba` placed at the root of this
directory.

```sh
# 1. Regenerate the cart dispatch code from the ROM + game.toml
../gbarecomp/build/gba_recompile --rom totkol.gba --config game.toml --out generated

# 2. Configure + build the actual game executable
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja
cmake --build build --target KnightOfLodisRecomp -j 8

# 3. Run it — headless, capped to N frames, dumping a screenshot at exit
./build/KnightOfLodisRecomp --rom totkol.gba --bios ../gbarecomp/bios/gba_bios.bin \
    --no-window --frames 600 --dump-bmp out.bmp

# ...or with a real window:
./build/KnightOfLodisRecomp --rom totkol.gba --bios ../gbarecomp/bios/gba_bios.bin
```

`src/main.cpp` is intentionally almost empty — the shared runtime's
`gbarecomp::run_game()` owns ROM/BIOS loading, hash verification, the
CPU/bus/PPU/audio/host-window setup, and the main loop. The per-game
binary only supplies the generated dispatch table (linked in via
`CMakeLists.txt`) and a couple of built-in identity strings.

After any run, check the exit banner (`self_heal_coverage=...
dispatch_misses=N`) and, if `N > 0`, the auto-generated
`recomp_master_misses_ATOE.toml.frag` next to the executable. Review it,
then hand-merge the genuine cart-ROM entries into `game.toml` (see the
worked example already in that file) — never anything at a `0x03xxxxxx`
RAM address, and never auto-merge. Regenerate, rebuild, re-run.

## Real hardware verification (started 2026-09-17)

Cart-ROM coverage is fully static through 9000 frames (~150s), RAM
self-heal aside. The next question was never coverage — it was whether
"looks right" is actually "matches real hardware." That verification
loop is now set up and has already found and fixed one real bug:

- Built the mGBA-backed oracle: cloned `third_party/mgba` at tag 0.10.5,
  built `libmgba`, then `gbarecomp`'s own `gbarecomp_oracle` target
  (`-DGBARECOMP_BUILD_ORACLE=ON`). This is a real, independent GBA core
  running behind a TCP protocol, kept as a strictly separate binary from
  the native build (libmgba is MPL-2.0; the shipped executable never
  links it).
- Wrote `oracle_diff/diff_frame_totkol.py`, a copy of
  `gbarecomp/oracle/diff_frame.py` adapted to drive this project's own
  executable + ROM (the original only knows how to drive gbarecomp's
  BIOS-only `bios_smoke` tool). Same protocol, same sync discipline —
  steps both sides one PPU frame at a time and diffs the framebuffer
  plus OAM/PAL/VRAM/EWRAM/IWRAM/IO byte-for-byte, reporting the first
  divergent byte in each.
- **First run immediately found a real bug — not in this game's config,
  in the shared framework.** At frame 0, before either side executes a
  single guest instruction, the native framebuffer read solid black
  while the oracle read solid white. Root cause: `GbaIo`'s constructor
  in `gbarecomp/src/gba/gba_io.cpp` left `DISPCNT` at 0 instead of the
  real GBA power-on default `0x0080` (Forced Blank set) — cross-checked
  directly against mGBA's own source. The PPU already implements
  forced-blank rendering correctly; the register just never had the bit
  set to begin with. Fixed upstream in `gbarecomp` (not here — this was
  a framework bug, affecting every game built on it, not a Knight of
  Lodis-specific issue). Verified with gbarecomp's full 26-test ctest
  suite (still 26/26) and before/after oracle diffs: frame 0's
  framebuffer, OAM, PAL, VRAM, EWRAM and IWRAM are now all
  byte-identical to the oracle (previously only EWRAM matched).
- **The three remaining "divergences" were chased down individually.
  None of them are execution bugs; two are expected hardware quirks
  neither emulator needs to "fix," and one was a flaw in the comparison
  itself, now corrected.**
  - **`DISPSTAT`'s VCounter status bit at frame 0** — native computes it
    live on every read (`vcount() == target`); mGBA only updates it via
    a scheduled event at each scanline transition, so at the artificial
    "before either core has ticked once" instant, native has already
    computed the match while mGBA hasn't gotten there yet. Read mGBA's
    own `_startHdraw` in `third_party/mgba/src/gba/video.c` to confirm.
    No real game reads this bit before its first real scanline event
    fires, so this doesn't affect anything — deliberately left alone.
  - **`BG0HOFS` (and the whole class of scroll/affine/DMA-address
    registers) reading differently** — these are *write-only* on real
    GBA hardware. Confirmed with a native memory-write watchpoint
    (`GBARECOMP_ABORT_ON_MEM_WRITE_ADDR=0x04000010`) that this address
    is **never written** in 120 frames on our side, so the "difference"
    was never about a wrong stored value. Reading a write-only register
    on real hardware returns open-bus garbage; mGBA models this exactly
    (`GBALoadBad()`, confirmed in `third_party/mgba/src/gba/io.c` —
    it's the documented write-only-register case, not a bug), while
    gbarecomp just returns a fixed value. A real, if obscure, hardware-
    fidelity gap in gbarecomp — but no legitimate game logic ever reads
    a write-only register expecting real data, so this has zero
    practical effect and wasn't fixed.
  - **A one-frame query-alignment offset — this was the real one, and
    it explains everything else.** Verified across 20+ consecutive
    frames: `native`'s snapshot at frame *N* is **exactly** byte-
    identical to the oracle's snapshot at frame *N+1*, for every region
    that actually changes per frame (confirmed on an IWRAM counter and
    on OAM). This is native's `frame` command reporting `vblank_count`
    (incremented at a different point in the main loop than mGBA's own
    frame counter) — a comparison-harness convention mismatch, not a
    CPU or game-logic bug. `diff_frame_totkol.py` now takes it into
    account: it steps the oracle one extra frame ahead by default
    (`--oracle-lead 1`; pass `0` to see the old, misleading picture).
  - **With that compensation applied, the real result:** OAM, PAL,
    VRAM, and EWRAM are byte-identical to the oracle across every frame
    checked from 0 to 120 (dense scan, every 15th frame). The only
    remaining differences are the two understood-and-inconsequential
    ones above (`DISPSTAT` bit, write-only-register reads). This is a
    real, meaningful verification result: actual game state — not just
    "what it looks like" — matches independent reference hardware
    emulation through the whole tested boot window.

## Call-return stack crash: ROOT-CAUSED AND FIXED (2026-09-17)

The crash that ended real play sessions after a few minutes is fixed. It
had **two** independent causes, both now addressed, and the evidence for
each is below. Earlier revisions of this file chased several wrong
theories and prematurely called one partial fix complete; that history is
summarized honestly at the end rather than deleted.

**Cause 1 — the forced unwind orphaned call-return frames (the leak).**
Every generated function begins each instruction with
`if (runtime_should_yield()) return;` — a BARE return that pops nothing.
`runtime_should_yield` forces an unwind once the tracked call depth
reaches `kPresentInPlaceCallDepthLimit` (512), tearing down the whole
generated host call chain so the runner can re-dispatch the published PC.
But the corresponding call-return frames were never retired, so one
tear-down stranded the entire chain. Worse, this is self-reinforcing:
the depth is now pinned above 512, so every later frame re-triggers the
same unwind. That exactly matches the measured signature — depth sat
pinned at 3 for thousands of calls, then climbed to ~567 (just past 512)
and **stuck** there, after which pushes and matches tracked 1:1.
Fixed by publishing the depth the runner entered dispatch at
(`g_runtime_dispatch_base_depth`) and truncating back to it on both
forced-unwind exits. Truncating is safe: a later guest return that no
longer finds its frame simply falls through to a full `runtime_dispatch`,
which is the designed slow path, not a wrong one.

**Cause 2 — the 1024-entry buffer was genuinely too small.** With the
leak fixed, an instrumented run measured the game's real peak call depth
at **6,153** — a transient spike that then unwinds completely back to 0.
That is legitimate deep recursion in this ROM (consistent with the
MP2K-shaped recursive cluster in `0x0815A000`-`0x0815A400`), not a
defect. The original `kCallReturnStackSize = 1024` simply could not hold
it. The earlier raise to 65536 — described at the time as a band-aid —
was in fact necessary, and this measurement is what justifies it.

**Verification after the fix** (all clean, all re-run from scratch):

| Check | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Light casual input, 12,202 frames | climbed to 574 orphaned frames | **zero growth** |
| Crash reproducer (`repro_callstack_crash.py`) | SIGABRT at frame 2618 | **runs clean to 9,950** |
| Aggressive mashing, 56,360 frames (~16 min game time) | crashed | **zero growth, no crash** |
| Instrumented 42,710-frame run | depth stuck ~567 | **depth 0 at every sample**, peak 6,153 then fully unwinds |
| gbarecomp ctest | 26/26 | **26/26** |
| Idle 9,000-frame baseline | — | **unchanged** |
| mGBA oracle diff (OAM/PAL/VRAM/EWRAM) | — | **still byte-identical** |

**Caveat on the diagnostic threshold.** `GBARECOMP_CALL_STACK_ABORT_AT`
was useful for forcing a fast repro, but any value below ~6,200 will now
false-trip on the game's legitimate deep recursion. A run with
`--abort-at 300` still "crashes" for exactly that reason — that is the
diagnostic firing correctly, not the bug. Leave it unset for normal use.

**Two further real defects were found and fixed along the way**, neither
of which turned out to be the dominant cause, but both genuine:
`runtime_call_cancel_return` only inspected the top stack slot while its
counterpart `should_return` searches `[floor, depth)` (so any leftover
above a cancelled frame silently orphaned it, and because the cancel
cascade propagates upward, one blocked level blocked all of them); and
the self-heal bridge cleanup could *resurrect* already-retired frames by
restoring upward, a bug introduced earlier in this same investigation.

**Hypotheses tested and cleanly eliminated** (recorded so they are not
re-chased): a stranded IRQ floor (diagnostic showed the only hits had an
interrupt genuinely active — the floor doing its job); a missing static
coverage entry at `0x0815938a` (real gap, seeded in `game.toml`, zero
effect on the leak); and the idea that push-minus-match is a leak count
(it is not — truncation-by-outer-return is invisible to it, which
misled an earlier pass; read the depth column instead).

## Sprite fade bug: FIXED (2026-09-17)

Reported from play-testing: during a fade, sprites did not fade with the
rest of the scene — they stayed at full brightness while the backgrounds
darkened/brightened around them.

Root cause was in the framework, not this game. Both compositing paths
in `gbarecomp/src/gba/gba_ppu.cpp` decided whether an OBJ pixel is a
color-special-effects *first target* with `blend_enabled(ux) && obj_mode
== 1`, which only admits semi-transparent sprites and ignores BLDCNT
bit 4 (OBJ) entirely. Backgrounds in the same function correctly test
`first_targets & (1u << layer)`, and the adjacent OBJ *second*-target
test already read `second_targets & (1u << 4)` — only the first-target
test was missing its bit check. Fixed upstream in gbarecomp (commit
`fc961e5`); sprites now fade in step with the scene, confirmed by
play-testing.

This game's own register dumps confirm it is a legitimate trigger:
BLDCNT reads `0x3f5f` / `0x1f5f` (alpha blend, OBJ 1st target) and
`0x3fbf` (brightness increase, OBJ 1st target) during the intro.

**Verification honesty — the oracle diff did not catch this.** A full
revert/rebuild/re-run A/B moved the summed whole-frame pixel difference
vs mGBA over frames 100-300 by only 52174 -> 52059. The sprite pixels
were swamped by unrelated divergences in the same frames. The fix rests
on the hardware-behavior argument plus direct visual confirmation, not
on that number. Lesson for future work: whole-frame difference *sums*
are a poor detector for a localized rendering defect — diff a bounded
region, or a specific layer, when chasing one.

**FIXED 2026-09-18 — semi-transparent OBJs were taking the brightness
effect.** Reported as UI icons (the hand, the END text) being darkened as if
in the shadow of other sprites. Reproduced from `states/R_objprio.state`, where the
game sets `BLDCNT=0x3FD0` (OBJ the only 1st target, effect 3 brightness
decrease, every layer a 2nd target) with `BLDY=8` and `BLDALPHA=0x0010`.

Three "END" banners sit over units that have finished their turn. Two rendered
white-on-black; the third rendered grey-on-grey, darkened by exactly `BLDY=8`
(`FFFFEF` -> `847B7B`, `101008` -> `080808`). The only thing distinguishing it:
that banner overlapped another sprite.

Two defects in the blend resolver, both in `gba_ppu.cpp`, in both copies of the
pipeline (faithful and extended-view):

1. The alpha branch was gated on `top[x].layer == 4` — "the top pixel is an
   OBJ" — where GBATEK means "a *semi-transparent* OBJ". OBJ mode was never
   carried onto the pixel candidate. So a **normal-mode** OBJ that was a 1st
   target took the alpha path (here EVA=16/EVB=0, the identity) instead of the
   brightness path, and never darkened.
2. A semi-transparent OBJ with no valid 2nd target below fell *through* to the
   brightness branch. Per GBATEK semi-transparent OBJs are "always using Alpha
   Blending mode (regardless of BLDCNT Bit 6-7)", so the effect bits must never
   reach them; with no 2nd target the sprite renders unmodified. OBJ-over-OBJ
   is excluded from blending, which is exactly how the third END banner lost
   its 2nd target and got darkened.

The fix adds a `semi` flag to `PixelCandidate`, sets it from OBJ mode 1, gates
the alpha branch on it, and excludes it from the brightness branch.

Both defects were visible in this one frame, in opposite directions. Defect 1
was suppressing a *wanted* effect: the command menu greys out unavailable
options via mode-0 sprites plus this same BLDCNT, and all three icons were
being drawn bright. Defect 2 was applying an *unwanted* one to the END banner.
Fixing both makes the menu grey out its two disabled entries and the three END
banners render identically.

Scale of the change, measured against a pre-fix binary across all 18 states in
`states/`: **17 are byte-identical**; only `R_objprio` moves, by 736 pixels
confined to x 97-191, y 50-119. 501 of those go darker (defect 1 — the two
disabled menu icons, now greyed as intended) and 235 go brighter (defect 2),
every one of the 235 at a sprite-over-sprite overlap.

This fix deliberately breaks render invariant 1 (faithful 240x160 byte-identical
to a pre-change build) — correcting the faithful path is the whole point — which
is why the change is quantified above rather than merely asserted. Invariant 2
was re-checked and still holds: centre-240 byte-identical at width 320 with
`KOL_WS_NO_HUD_ANCHOR=1 KOL_WS_NO_PANEL_PIN=1`, on all 18 states.

Regression test: `test_semitransparent_obj_ignores_brightness_effect` in
`tests/ppu_smoke/test_main.cpp`, built from the game's own register values.
Each of its assertions was checked to fail with its guard reverted.

**This was never the extended view.** Verified before hunting: with the
extended-view features off the centre 240x160 is byte-identical to the faithful
render, and with them on the differing pixels sit entirely in y 0..71 over the
terrain box and HP/MP cluster — nowhere near the menu or the END labels.

*An earlier version of this entry concluded the renderer was "doing what the
registers say" and that settling it needed the oracle. That was wrong, and it
was wrong because the reasoning stopped at the frame-level registers instead of
asking why three identical banners rendered two different ways. The register
decode was right; the conclusion drawn from it was not.*

**STILL OPEN, and unaffected by the fix:** frames 220-268 run a
brightness-increase effect with OBJ targeted (`BLDCNT=0x3fbf`) and show
a rock-steady ~3622-pixel difference against mGBA, byte-identical with
and without the sprite fix. A separate defect in the same area of the
PPU. Not diagnosed — the pixels' on-screen location has not been mapped
yet. Do not assume the sprite fix covered it.

That item is now a plausible candidate for the **same** defect. `0x3fbf` names
every layer including OBJ as 1st target with effect 2 (brightness increase), so
defect 1 above would have suppressed the brightening on every normal-mode
sprite — which would read as a steady, frame-stable pixel difference of exactly
that kind. This is a hypothesis, not a result: the oracle is not built in this
checkout, so it has not been re-run. Do not close the item on this note.

## Android port (2026-09-17/18)

Runs natively on an **AYN Thor** (arm64-v8a, Android 13, Snapdragon 8 Gen 2).
This is the framework's supported Android path (`gbarecomp/README.md` "Android"),
not a fork.

### Toolchain

| Component | Version |
|---|---|
| NDK | `27.3.13750724` (r27 LTS) |
| cmdline-tools | 19.0 (12.0 is TOO OLD — cannot parse this SDK's XML v4) |
| CMake | 3.22.1 (SDK-provided) |
| JDK | 17 |
| Gradle / AGP | 8.7 / 8.5.2 |
| SDL2 | 2.32.10, vendored at `android/app/jni/SDL` (gitignored) |

SDL2 is fetched, not committed:

```sh
curl -L -o SDL2.tar.gz \
  https://github.com/libsdl-org/SDL/releases/download/release-2.32.10/SDL2-2.32.10.tar.gz
tar xzf SDL2.tar.gz && mv SDL2-2.32.10 android/app/jni/SDL
```

Its Java glue (`android/app/src/main/java/org/libsdl/app/*.java`) IS committed,
because the APK needs it and the SDL checkout is not.

### Building

```sh
cd android && ./gradlew assembleDebug      # ~70 s for the native side
adb install -r app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk
```

Measured: 18 generated shards, 13 s each, **71 s** full native build, **37 MB**
stripped `libmain.so`. The 202 MB / 38,217-function scale was expected to be the
main risk and turned out not to be a problem at all.

**Gradle gotcha (load-bearing).** AGP builds *every* CMake target by default,
which pulls in gbarecomp's host-side test generators (`gen_codegen_tests` et
al), cross-compiles them to arm64 and then fails trying to run them on the build
machine. `app/build.gradle` sets `targets 'main'` to prevent this. Do not
remove it.

### Android-specific constraints

- **Self-heal recompilation must be OFF.** Android has no runtime C toolchain
  and blocks `dlopen` of app-written `.so` files; the bundled tcc has no arm64
  backend. `main_android.cpp` sets `GBARECOMP_SELFHEAL_RECOMPILE=0`. What the
  static build misses stays interpreted for the whole session — loudly
  logged, as the project rules require. Since 2026-10-06 that is no IWRAM
  code in any saved state, and ~117 interpreted instructions a frame on
  most (README "Two more IWRAM copies, found by a sweep").
- **SDLThread's stack is ~1 MB** (measured: 1,072,304 bytes) against a desktop
  main thread's 8 MB. The save-state serializer overflowed it and killed the
  process with `SIGSEGV / "stack pointer is not in a rw map"` inside
  `SnapshotWriter::u16` under `GbaPpu::serialize`. `main_android.cpp` now runs
  `run_game()` on a pthread with a **16 MB** stack. Fixed upstream too: a
  gratuitous 112 KB `std::array` framebuffer on the stack in
  `GbaPpu::serialize` is now heap-allocated.
- **stdout/stderr are routed to logcat** (tag `KoL`) by `main_android.cpp`.
  Without this the runtime's entire diagnostic surface — coverage banner,
  dispatch misses, save-state results — is silently discarded, which turns any
  Android failure into guesswork. `adb logcat -s KoL` now shows what a desktop
  terminal would. This is what made the stack-overflow crash findable.
- **Raise the log ring before instrumenting: `adb logcat -G 16M`.** The Thor
  ships a 256 KiB main ring, which on a busy device spans about THIRTY SECONDS.
  This app out-logs that on its own — one hover fires dozens of excursions, each
  printing three lines — so its output is pruned before it can be read, and the
  startup banner goes with it. The symptom is not a truncated log, it is
  `adb logcat -s KoL` returning NOTHING while the game is plainly running, which
  reads as "logging is broken" or "the code never ran". It cost most of a
  session. 16 MiB holds a full run.

### Verification

- Framebuffer **byte-for-byte identical** to the macOS arm64 build at frame 600.
- **5.00x realtime** headless (1800 frames in 6 s) on the Thor.
- BIOS and ROM both hash-verify on device.

### Presentation

No on-screen touch controls (`GBARECOMP_TOUCH_CONTROLS=0`): the Thor has real
buttons. With them off the picture fills the display at the GBA's 3:2 aspect —
`min(w/240, h/160)`, so a 16:9 landscape panel fills vertically (1620x1080 on
1080p) and a portrait one fills horizontally. Deliberately NOT snapped to an
integer multiple; snapping to 6x on 1080p would waste 11% of the height. Pass
`--sharp-filter` if the non-integer scaling looks uneven.

### ROM/BIOS provisioning

`SetupActivity` is the launcher: it file-picks the ROM and BIOS, copies them to
app-private storage and reports their SHA-1s. Nothing copyrighted is in the APK.
`MainActivity` is `exported=false`, so `am start` on it is refused — go through
`SetupActivity`.

Dev shortcut for a debug build:

```sh
adb shell "run-as com.koldecomp.game sh -c 'mkdir -p files && \
  cat /data/local/tmp/kol/totkol.gba > files/totkol.gba && \
  cat /data/local/tmp/kol/gba_bios.bin > files/gba_bios.bin'"
```

### Playing without a BIOS (opt-in, experimental, 2026-10-18)

The BIOS stays sacred: the recompiled real BIOS is the default and the only
oracle. For players without a dump there is an opt-in mode, `--no-bios`
(`[bios] none = true`, `GBARECOMP_NO_BIOS=1`; on Android the setup screen's
"Play without a BIOS (experimental)" box, which writes `files/no_bios`). There
is no BIOS file at all: gbarecomp's `BiosHleMode::NoBios` serves the SWIs from
`bios_hle.cpp`, runs native stand-ins for the only two BIOS addresses reached
outside a SWI (the IRQ vector `0x18` and the IRQ wrapper's return `0x138`),
sets the four open-bus values mGBA uses, and stops with a message on anything
else. The intro is skipped. Fast Loading now chains to an installed HLE hook
instead of switching itself off.

**What KoL needs from the BIOS** (ROM scan + `GBARECOMP_SWI_LOG`): wrappers for
SWIs 0x06 0x08 0x0A 0x0B 0x0C 0x0E 0x0F 0x11 0x12 0x13 at `0x08158EEC..F20`, all
in the HLE layer, and 0x2A at `0x0815C838`, never called (MP2K uses its own
table in ROM). No Halt/IntrWait/VBlankIntrWait: KoL never waits on the BIOS.

**Measured** (the Mac, real BIOS with `--skip-bios-intro` vs `--bios-hle` vs
`--no-bios`): cold boot f1500, AB +600, the mash replay to f8000, AB and AF
with A pressed: final frames identical in all three. `--no-bios` is
byte-identical to `--bios-hle` in IWRAM everywhere, so the IRQ stand-ins match
the BIOS wrapper exactly. HLE as a whole is not identical to the real BIOS: its
SWIs charge different cycles (~25k cycles over 2.2 G in the mash run), which
shifts counters and the sound state; on the FN View List round trip the HLE
decompressors finish each load ~17 frames sooner (map ready at frame 223, not
240), the same scene otherwise. That is what the experimental warning is for.
Both render invariants unchanged on the default path (66e13ab2, 9054c456).

Not done: the binary still links `bios_recompiled.cpp` (generated from the
developer's dump), so a release build without BIOS-derived code needs it left
out; there is no desktop UI for the mode (flag/config only); on Android the
setup screen launches straight into the game once provisioned, so the box can
only be changed by clearing `files/no_bios`.

### Save-state controls

**L3+R1 saves slot 1, L3+L1 loads slot 1.** L3 is a modifier, so while held the
shoulder buttons are withheld from the guest (otherwise every save would also
press GBA R). Edge-triggered. Added because F1..F9 need a keyboard and the
long-press runtime menu only exists in `GBARECOMP_RUNTIME_UI` builds, which this
APK is not.

---

## Second screen: live character panel (2026-09-18)

The Thor exposes its second panel as an ordinary Android presentation display
(`dumpsys display`: `Display 4 "Screen-2", 1240x1080, FLAG_PRESENTATION`), so
`android.app.Presentation` targets it with no vendor SDK and it degrades to a
no-op on single-screen devices.

**You cannot mirror the game's own status screen.** The GBA has one PPU and one
framebuffer; while combat is on the main screen the status screen is not being
drawn anywhere. The panel is *rebuilt* from guest memory instead — which is also
why it can be laid out for 1240x1080 rather than upscaled from 240x160.

Strictly a **present-time shadow**: `runtime_ewram_view()` (added to the
framework) hands out a READ-ONLY window on guest EWRAM. It never writes, never
feeds back into emulation, is never a verify oracle. See PRINCIPLES.md
"Verified-enhancement HLE is permitted".

**JNI gotcha (cost an hour):** `FindClass` on a natively-attached pthread
resolves against the *system* classloader and cannot see application classes.
The class ref and method id must be resolved on **SDLThread** (Java created it,
so it carries the app classloader); only the `JNIEnv` is per-thread.

### Unit record map (EWRAM)

```
0x02028960   u32 -> record of the CURRENTLY SELECTED/HIGHLIGHTED unit
  +0x30  name, 0xFF-terminated
  +0x40  u16 HP cur, HP max, MP cur, MP max, STR, INT, AGI
  +0x52  u8  level
```

Text encoding: `'A'-'Z' = 0x00..0x19`, `'a'-'z' = 0x1A..0x33`, `0xFF` terminates.

Unit array stride **0x68**; Alphonse idx 0 at `0x02001420`, Rictor idx 12 at
`0x02001900`. (This said stride `0x4E0` and idx 1 until 2026-09-20. It was
wrong, and it hid every unit but two — see "Second screen: the unit panel,
read from the record and ROM" for the full record layout.)

How the pointer was found, because the method generalises: two static per-unit
copies exist and *neither* follows the cursor. Searching for any 32-bit value
that shifted by exactly the array stride between two save states returned
**exactly one** candidate. Verified on three units (Alphonse Lv1, Rictor Lv3,
Justin Lv2).

Class-name strings: pointer table at ROM `0x623678`, 4 bytes/entry, into a
`0xFF`-separated pool. id 9 = Soldier, 10 Ninja, 11 Archer, 12 Wizard,
13 Cleric, 14 Knight, 15 Swordmaster, 21 Priest, 24 Hawkman, 40 Naga.
Compound names such as "High Priest" are `<81>xx` dictionary escapes and need a
decoder that has not been written.

### Second screen: the game's own glyphs (2026-09-18)

The unit panel renders "Lv.", "HP:", "MP:", every number and the unit's name
with the **game's own tiles**, while keeping the HP/MP progress bars the game
does not have.

**Panel text is one tile per character**, and the mapping is fixed:

| Glyph | Tile | Palette bank |
|---|---|---|
| digit `d` | `0x56 + d` | 4 |
| `HP:` | `0xA8, 0xA9` | 12 |
| `MP:` | `0xAA, 0xAB` | 13 |
| `Lv.` | `0xB3, 0xB4` | 12 |
| `EXP` | `0xB5, 0xB6` | 12 |

All out of BG2's char block (base 2 on the battle map, 16-colour).

Verified by reading the tilemap under known values rather than by eye:
Brigitte Lv1 HP130 gives tiles `57,59,56`, and Rictor Lv3 HP172 gives
`57,5D,58`. Three states, exact.

**The per-label palette bank matters.** MP is bank 13 and HP is bank 12, which
is why they come out pink and blue exactly as in the game; taking one bank for
the whole atlas would have flattened that.

`capture_font_atlas()` rasterises these into an 80x16 atlas — row 0 digits, row
1 labels — sent to Java once, and the view blits from it at an integer scale.

**The name is different and has to be an image.** The game renders names into a
*dynamically allocated contiguous run* of tiles (`0x21F, 0x220, 0x221 …`, two
tiles per character for 8x16 glyphs), not by indexing a static font by
character code. So there is no code -> tile mapping to find for names;
`capture_unit_name()` takes the 64x16 rect out of BG2 instead.

**STR:/INT:/AGI: come from the status screen.** They are not in the unit
panel's tiles at all. On the status screen they sit on **BG1**, char block 2,
palette bank 12:

| Label | Tiles |
|---|---|
| `STR` | `0x168, 0x169` |
| `INT` | `0x16B, 0x16C` |
| `AGI` | `0x16D, 0x16E` |

all sharing the colon tile `0x16A`. Verified by reading the values beside them:
`58,5A` = 24, `57,58` = 12, `58,56` = 20, matching the unit's stats — and the
digits are the same `0x56 + d` tiles as everywhere else.

The panel's glyph rendering is gated on having captured the frame. The digits
are palette bank 4, near-black, drawn for the game's cream panel — without it
behind them they are invisible on the dark card, so the panel falls back to
ordinary text until a unit panel has been seen once.

**They are not resident during battle.** That char region holds different data
on the battle map, checked against five battle states, so they cannot simply be
rendered by index there. `capture_status_labels()` fires while the status
screen is up (`is_status_scene()`, which classifies on BG0/BG1 drawing from
char block 2 — the same clause that separates it from the battle map) and the
view caches the result. Until the player has opened a status screen once, the
panel falls back to ordinary text.

**The panel is recoloured per team.** The frame tiles are the same indices
(`0x001..0x020`); only the palette bank changes — 4 for the player's cream
panel, 5 for the green one another team gets. So the frame is re-sent whenever
its pixels change rather than captured once, which is what an earlier version
got wrong: enemy units rendered in friendly colours. The glyph atlas stays
one-shot, because digits are bank 4 and labels banks 12/13 in both — confirmed
byte-identical across a friendly and an other-team capture, not assumed.

### Second screen: the unit panel wears the game's furniture (2026-09-18)

The rebuilt unit stats now sit in the **game's own panel**, 9-sliced from its
tiles, while keeping the HP/MP progress bars the game does not have.

The frame comes free from a fact established for panel pinning: the unit info
panel is a solid 10x7 block on **BG3**, and its text and icons live on **BG2**.
So rasterising BG3 alone over that rect yields the empty cream box — border,
hatch and all — with no contents. `capture_unit_panel_frame()` does exactly
that, and it is sent to Java once.

The 9-slice takes corners from the frame's four corners and tiles edges and
centre from clean 8px patches deliberately chosen to miss the **icon well** the
game draws in its bottom-left, which would otherwise smear across the whole
background. The hatch is 8-periodic, so tiling 8px patches is seamless — the
same property the bottom-bar continuation relies on.

Ink is **sampled from the frame**, not guessed: the darkest opaque pixel in the
panel becomes the text colour, so the type belongs to the same palette as the
furniture.

Two bugs worth recording, both found on the device rather than in review:

- The first ink scan read only the frame's **first row**, which is fully
  transparent. No opaque pixel was found, ink stayed white, and the result was
  white text on a cream panel. Scan the whole bitmap.
- The panel border is 3 guest pixels — **24 device pixels at 8x** — and the
  first layout ran the text under it. Contents need an explicit inset past the
  border, not just the panel's own padding.

### Second screen: terrain panel (2026-09-18)

The second screen carries the game's **own terrain box**, mirrored: elevation
("6 STEP"), the terrain icon, the six elemental modifiers, and the defence /
attack figures — everything the top-right box shows, pixel-exact.

It is rasterised straight out of the UI tilemaps, not rebuilt from values.
`capture_terrain_box()` composites BG3 (frame) then BG2 (contents) over the
box's tile rect — cols 23..29 x rows 0..8, 56x72 px, stable across every
sampled state — and `main_android.cpp` pushes the ARGB to
`SecondScreen.pushTerrainBox`, where it is drawn at an integer scale (9x on the
Thor's 1240x1080 panel).

**This does not contradict "you cannot mirror the status screen" above.** That
holds because the status screen is not drawn during combat — one PPU, one
framebuffer. The terrain box *is* on screen, so its tiles are live in VRAM.

**Why mirror this one when the unit panel is rebuilt.** Elevation and the
terrain icon are per-tile, not per-terrain-type, so neither is in the ROM
record that the terrain id resolves — and the per-tile structure was never
found (see below). Mirroring delivers all of it exactly and drops that hunt
off the critical path. The trade is upscaled pixel art instead of a native
1240x1080 layout, which is a weak cost for an icon-and-orb box and a strong one
for the text-heavy unit stats — hence the split.

Read from the **tilemap, not the framebuffer**, so HUD anchoring and panel
pinning — which move where the box is presented — cannot affect it.

**The box STAYS on the main screen**, at the top right where the game puts it.
It is mirrored on the second screen as well; the two are not exclusive.

An earlier version suppressed it on the main screen once the presentation
bound, on the reasoning that the second screen now carried it and the
battlefield could show through. That was **removed on request 2026-09-20** —
the box is wanted where the game draws it — and removed rather than switched
off: the flag, the setter, the `KOL_WS_HIDE_TERRAIN_BOX` switch, the per-cell
map, the tile-identity matcher and the `main_android.cpp` call are all gone.
Do not reintroduce it behind a default-off flag.

One fact from that work is worth keeping, because it is about the GAME and not
about the removed feature: **the terrain box relocates.** With a NAVI bar up it
is drawn at BG3 columns 15..21 instead of its usual 23..29. Anything that has
to find it by position must cope with that; the second-screen mirror below uses
the fixed rect and handles the other case by gating on what is actually drawn
there.

**Gated on the box actually being there.** The capture rect is a fixed screen
position, not something the game owns, so whatever else it draws there lands in
the capture. A NAVI dialogue ("Choose where you want to move this character")
overwrites rows 2..7 of that rect with its own tiles, and the second screen
duly showed the dialogue over the terrain readout. The game itself occludes its
own terrain box the same way — the main screen at 240 shows it cut off, which
is faithful, not a bug.

The discriminator is the six **element orb tiles `0xA2..0xA7`**, which the box
always draws whatever the values are. Require all six in the rect and the
capture refuses otherwise; the second screen then keeps the last good one.
Checked across every state: present in the three with a terrain box, absent in
the occluded one and in the four with no box at all — which also means earlier
builds were capturing fragments in those.

The same test gates the **main-screen suppression**, or hiding would punch a
hole in the dialogue. Verified both ways: with the dialogue up, hiding is a
byte-for-byte no-op; with a real box, it still hides.

**Gated on the battle-map classifier.** Off the battle map those tiles hold
something else: on the title screen the same rect rasterised to intro graphics,
which is worse than showing nothing. `capture_terrain_box()` returns false
unless `kol::is_battle_scene()` is true, which is the same DISPCNT + BGxCNT
classifier the extended-view scene policy uses, so the two cannot drift.
Verified both ways: a battle state captures byte-identically to before the
gate, and a 3000-frame cold boot through the intro captures nothing at all.

The terrain id is still tracked (shown as "id N") through the accessor hook,
because it is free once the hook is installed and it names the record.

`KOL_TERRAIN_BOX_DUMP=<path.bmp>` writes one rasterised box to disk, which is
how the compositing was checked against a rendered frame before any of it went
near the device.

Three layout traps on the Thor's second panel, which is 1240x1080:

- The unit and terrain sections must draw independently. An early `return` in
  `onDraw` for "no unit selected" hid the terrain block entirely.
- Stacking the box under the unit stats capped it at 3x, because a 56x72 box
  is height-limited and that layout wasted the panel's width. A column of its
  own gets it to 9x.
- Going two-column clipped the unit panel's "base values" note under the
  terrain column; it needed shortening and resizing to the left column.

### Second screen: the unit panel, read from the record and ROM (2026-09-20)

The panel shows the hovered unit's name, class, level, EXP, HP/MP, the
equipment-adjusted STR/INT/AGI, the melee and magic attack figures, and the
four equipment and four talent slots. **None of it is captured.** It is read
out of the unit record and a handful of ROM tables, so it is exact and
immediate for every unit on the map, including ones the player has never
looked at.

That replaced a speculative-capture path — fork the machine, press B in a
discarded timeline, let the guest draw the window, decode the rendered tilemap,
rewind — which is now **deleted** (`src/kol_status_mirror.cpp`, and with it
`files/autostatus.cfg` and `files/excdump.cfg`). It worked, but it cost a fork
per never-seen unit, and everything it recovered turned out to be readable
directly. The framework seam it used (`gbarecomp/ENHANCEMENTS.md` §4,
speculative excursions and shadow timelines) is untouched and still supported;
nothing in this game uses it any more.

#### The unit record

**The stride is `0x68` (104 bytes), and the roster is contiguous from
`0x02001420`.** An earlier note in this file said `0x4E0`, and that was wrong in
a way that hid the whole problem for several sessions: Alphonse is index 0 and
Rictor index 12, and those two happen to sit `0x4E0` apart, so a stride derived
from that one pair looked right and showed exactly two units. With `0x68` the
same state shows eight — the eight the device had been decoding all along.

```
+0x30  name, 0xFF-terminated ('A'-'Z' = 0x00.., 'a'-'z' = 0x1A.., space 0x89)
+0x40  u16 HP cur, HP max, MP cur, MP max, STR, INT, AGI   (BASE figures)
+0x50  class id -> class table
+0x52  u8  level
+0x53  u8  EXP
+0x60  four equipment ids -> item table
+0x64  four talent ids    -> talent table (0xFF = empty slot)
```

`0x02028960` still holds a pointer to the highlighted unit's record, and it is
**sticky**: it keeps naming the last unit the cursor stood on, so it is not
proof the cursor is on a unit. Cursor position itself is `0x0202AB90` (x) and
`0x0202AB91` (y).

#### The ROM tables

Each table holds a u16 name-pool id at entry offset 0.

| table | base | stride |
|---|---|---|
| class | `0x08615228` | 88 |
| item | `0x08616F60` | 36 |
| talent | `0x0861A8F0` | 64 |
| name pointers | `0x08623678` | 4 (489 entries) |

**Female class entries are sparse.** They carry a name and `+0x09`, the male
class id whose entry holds the real data, and nothing else. Resolve through it
before reading any class stat or a female unit reads zeros — which is also why
a search for "the offset that groups units by class name" finds the wrong
field: classes 1 and 2 are both "Soldier", so two Soldiers can hold different
ids.

Item entry fields: `+0x0C` PHYS (attack on a weapon, defence on armour),
`+0x0D` SPLL, `+0x13/+0x14/+0x15` STR/INT/AGI modifiers, `+0x0A` a category
(1 sword/shield/staff, 0 body armour/helmet, 5 bow).

Class entry fields: `+0x4C` damage-taken percent, `+0x53` innate (unarmed)
attack, `+0x54` weapon power percent.

#### `0x81 NN` is a BITMAP, not a dictionary

Roughly 40% of pool entries are a three-byte `81 NN FF`. This was assumed to be
a dictionary escape for compound names, and it is not: the game looks `NN` up
in a table at `0x0860D088` (stride 4: u16 tile offset, u16 cell count) and
blits **pre-rendered pixels** from `0x086A2AB0 + offset*32`, 4bpp, 64 bytes per
8x16 character cell. That is why "Tower Shield" and "High Priest" can never be
found as text anywhere in the ROM, and why the window draws these names into
dynamically allocated tile runs with no code->tile mapping.

Verified byte-exact: the ROM bytes for three of Alphonse's equipment names are
**identical** to the VRAM tiles the guest drew (512/384/512 bytes, zero
differing bytes). The panel carries them as a coverage mask and tints them,
rather than pasting the game's cream palette into a dark panel — the status
screen's palette is not even loaded while the battle map is up.

#### The figures the game "computes at draw time"

This file used to say the equipment-adjusted stats were "stored **nowhere**"
and that Move and the weapon figures were "almost certainly the same class of
derived value — do not go looking for addresses for them". The first half was
half right: the *results* are stored nowhere, but the *inputs* are all in ROM.

```
displayed STR/INT/AGI = record base + sum of the four items' +0x13/+0x14/+0x15
melee ATK = STR + (the stronger weapon's +0x0C, or class +0x53 with none) * class +0x54 / 100
magic ATK = the equipment-adjusted INT
```

One formula covers humans and beasts. Every human class has innate attack 5, so
an equipped weapon always wins; beasts and dragons carry no weapon and have
weapon power 100, so it collapses to `STR + innate` for them — which is the
community's separate "PA = STR + 50" beast rule, as a special case rather than
a second formula.

**Verified** against the rendered window on all eight units of
`Y_cursor_on_char.state`: zero mismatches on level, EXP, HP, the adjusted
stats, and melee ATK, and every class name identical.
