**Corrected 2026-09-29: which weapon.** Reported from the Thor: Deneb's ATK
was 215 on the second screen and 230 in the game's window
(`states/CS_deneb_attack.state`). The formula above was fitted on units
whose weapon sits in slot 1. Read from the game's routine `0x08139D1C`
(behind the 999 cap at `0x0813B094`):
- The weapons are the first two slots, in any position, whose item `+0x08`
  is 1 or 2 (`0x0813BEC0`).
- Each weapon's power is its `+0x0C`, or the class's innate attack when the
  item's kind `+0x06` is `0x0B`.
- The stronger one counts. With no weapon the innate attack counts, and it
  is not a floor under a weapon.

Deneb has a hat and a cloak in slots 1-2 and two wands in 3-4. Flauros also
changed, 195 to 199. Checked against the game's window, walked with
`KOL_NEXT_UNIT_AT` from Deneb's:
- Deneb 230;
- Flauros ATK 199 / DEF 717 / M.DEF 750;
- Eleanor 412 / 401 / 246;
- Tispee 522 / 580 / 278.

Eleanor's and Tispee's M.DEF were blank before the made-item fix.
`AW_alberich_mdef`'s 16 units and `CE_move_greyed`'s enemies are unchanged.

#### How these were found, and two traps on the way

Not by pattern-matching the ROM — by watching what the guest actually READ
while it drew a window, with `GBARECOMP_READ_WATCH="lo,hi[,max]"` (added to
`gbarecomp/src/runtime/runtime_bus_bridge.cpp`, the symmetric twin of the
existing `GBARECOMP_WRITE_WATCH`). Arm it on a unit record and the draw routine
reads the fields one after another at consecutive PCs; arm it on ROM and the
table lookups fall out with their indices.

- **Two plausible constant offsets fitted the first samples and were both
  wrong.** Equipment looked like `name_id = id + 40` (four of Rictor's four
  items fit) and talents like `id + 234` (both samples fit). Both are real
  tables whose first entries happen to line up. An offset that fits two points
  is not a finding.
- **Published community tables are fits, not readings.** A widely-cited weapon
  power table is uniformly one lower than the ROM (integer truncation makes
  `x*95/100` read as 94%); the defence table is the *inverse* of `+0x4C` and
  its bizarre "333%" entry is just `100/30`; and seven bespoke monster defence
  formulas are one formula with two bytes. They were excellent pointers to
  where to look and wrong in detail every time.

#### Defence — solved 2026-09-24, from the game's own routine

The sheet's DEF and M.DEF come from one routine, `0x08139FCC(unit, other,
flags, with_equipment)`, which the window calls twice (`flags` 0x41 physical,
0x42 magic, both with equipment on). Read from its disassembly, not fitted:

```
DEF   = 100 * (STR + sum of armour +0x0C + INNATE) / max(1, class +0x4C + trunc(sum item +0x16 / 2))
INNATE = class +0x53 when class +0x18 & 0x100 (the beasts and dragons), else 0
M.DEF = 100 * (INT + BUG) / max(1, (sum class +0x4D..+0x52 + trunc(sum items' +0x17..+0x1C / 2)) / 6)
BUG   = 4 * item[base INT & 0xFF].+0x0D
```

STR and INT are the equipment-adjusted figures. Armour is an item whose
`+0x06` is above 10. Item `+0x16..+0x1C` are SIGNED (`ldrsb`), and the halving
truncates toward zero. Class fields resolve through `+0x09` for sparse female
entries, as ATK's do.

- **The class term DIVIDES the whole sum, STR included.** That is why a Cleric
  (120% damage taken) shows DEF 20 on STR 21. A community formula circulating
  as "STR + armour × class modifier" is the right ingredients in the wrong
  shape; it cannot put DEF below STR.
- **Beasts add their innate attack.** The 20 classes with `+0x18 & 0x100`
  (36-48, 58, 82 among the real ones) are the beasts and dragons. This is
  where the community's seven "monster DEF" formulas come from.
- **The old fit missed on three-armour units because of `+0x16`**, a per-item
  damage-taken adjustment (-5 on heavy armour) that lowers the divisor.
  Alphonse's +5 was exactly that.
- **M.DEF has a guest bug, and the sheet shows its result.** The magic path's
  equipment loop at `0x0813A234` starts from a pointer the previous loop left
  at `sp+4` (the unit's base INT) and never advances it. So instead of the
  equipment's `+0x0D` it adds four times the `+0x0D` of the item whose ID is
  base INT's low byte. It is zero for every unit measured, and it is real:
  poking Alberich's base INT to 50 (his staff, `+0x0D` = 5) made the sheet read
  84, not the 63 a correct loop gives. The decode reproduces it.
- **Left unknown, not guessed** (the panel omits the figure): classes 64/65,
  whose fields resolve through a second ID. (Also once: a non-beast with
  `+0x4E == 0x18`, "a game flag". Decoded 2026-11-16 from Thor state 0302,
  where Shaher's DEF showed empty: 0x18 is Shaher's character id, and the flag is his
  story variant, byte `0x0200122C + 0x18` read through `0x08142FAC` at
  `0x0813A10E`; set, the class's innate (field 0x47) joins the DEF sum as a
  beast's does. It is 0 in 0302.)
- **Bug IDs above 0xC7 (decoded 2026-09-29).** These were left unknown, and
  every monster with a base INT of 200-255 lost its M.DEF on the sheet.
  Reported from the Thor on Radam (Cockatrice, base INT 216,
  `states/CR_mdef_missing.state`).
  - The loop reads through the item accessor `0x081437AC(id, 10, side)`. An
    ID above 0xC7 is made item `id - 0xC8`. The table is `0x02000D30`, or
    `0x02001C60` when the unit's `+0x5D` bit 5 is set (the routine's side
    flag, `0x08139FE6`). Field 10 is the `+0x0D` of that entry's base item
    (`+0x18`) in ROM (`0x08143960`).
  - Checked against the game's own window (`CE_move_greyed`, walked with
    `KOL_NEXT_UNIT_AT`): El Penoll (Vrtra, base INT 234) reads **248** and
    Raoduk (Red Dragon, base INT 201) **201**. Both match, and both were blank
    before. Radam now reads 236. The `other` pointer
  can also scale STR modifiers by 1.5 or 0.5. Its bytes were zero for the
  window, so it is not modelled.

**Verified** (humans) against the game's own sheet for all 16 party units of
`states/AW_alberich_mdef.state` (32 of 32 figures). The window only opens on
the unit under the cursor, so a TEST-ONLY entry hook handed the routine each
record in turn. The printed figure is therefore the game's own computation for
that unit. The hook was removed afterwards.

**How it was found:** `GBARECOMP_READ_WATCH` on one armour item's ROM entry
while the sheet drew gave the accessor PCs and their callers (`+0x0C` read from
`0x0813A0E1`, `+0x16` from `0x0813A175`). The callers are this routine. The
item accessor is a jump table at `0x08143800` (field n is entry offset n+3),
and the class accessor `0x0813FA44` is one at `0x0813FA78`. Read that literal
as the table base: the word before it is the pointer, and reading it as the
table shifts every case by one.

#### Element and alignment (2026-09-24)

The small square in the game's unit panel is the unit's **element** and the
letter beside it its **alignment**. Both are plain record bytes, found by
read-watching the record while the sheet drew:

```
+0x54  element    1 Earth, 2 Fire, 3 Wind, 4 Water, 5 Holy, 6 Dark
+0x55  alignment  1 Lawful, 2 Neutral, 3 Chaotic
```

The element order is the game's usual six (terrain modifiers, class
resistances). The icon is a 2x2 of BG tiles whose first tile comes from a u16
table at `0x0860DD2E` (0x7A, 0x7E, 0x82, 0x86, 0x8A, 0x8E), row-major. The
letter is tile `0xBF + alignment - 1`. Each tile's palette bank is a nibble in
a table at `0x086B7534` (routines at `0x0803B29C` and `0x0803B4BE`). An older
note in this file called tiles `0x86..0x89` "the element icon". They are the
water icon, which is what that unit had.

**Superseded the same day:** the second screen now draws the icon and
letter from the ROM, as part of the whole sheet ("The status sheet, from
ROM"). The VRAM capture described next was removed.

**The art came from VRAM, checksummed.** The pixels are not stored verbatim
in the ROM (the same custom codec as the sheet's other art), but all six
icons and three letters are resident in the battle map's panel tileset, BG
char block 2. `element_art_atlas()` reads them only when their CRC-32 matches
the art identified on `AW_alberich_mdef` (icons `0x9FF36A56`, letters
`0xAD88086B`), so anything else in those tiles fails closed. The palettes are
read from the ROM (banks 12/13 at `0x0861E0E8`/`0x0861E108`). The atlas is sent
to the panel once and drawn at 6x beside the class name. Until it arrives the
panel shows the names in text.

Checked against the game's own panel on four units: Alberich fire/L on
desktop, and Winter fire/N, Allos water/N and Alphonse fire/N on the device.

#### Still not solved

**Move**, and the **portrait** (it is an OBJ sprite, present in no tilemap, so
it could only ever come from a framebuffer capture).

#### Why the window still cannot simply be mirrored

Unchanged, and worth keeping: the status screen is a full SCENE SWITCH, not an
overlay (`is_status_screen()` keys on BG0/BG1 `char_base == 2`, where the
battle map uses block 0). One PPU, one framebuffer — while one is in VRAM the
other is not. That is why the old path had to fork rather than render, and why
the portrait cannot come back without one.


### Terrain properties table (ROM, 2026-09-18)

The battle map's top-right terrain panel — elevation, a terrain icon, and six
elemental modifiers — is driven by a table in ROM:

```
0x0861CA5C   terrain record base, stride 0x20, 89 records
  +0x16  6x s8  elemental modifiers, in order:
                orange, red, green, blue, white, grey
```

Screen layout is two columns of three; **memory order is row-major**, so it is
orange/red, then green/blue, then white/grey — not column-major.

Verified, not inferred: the modifier pattern for one sampled tile
(`+15,-10,-15,+10,+10,-10`, `0F F6 F1 0A 0A F6`) occurs **exactly once in the
entire 8 MiB ROM**, at `0x0861CA92` = record index 1, and decoding it against
that frame's on-screen panel matches position for position. A second state's
panel (`-10,0,+10,0,0,0`) then independently matches another record in the same
table with the same field order.

The base appears as a literal at 14+ call sites — `0x0804BFF4`, `0x0804C25C`,
`0x0804C448`, `0x0804C534`, `0x0804C5B0`, `0x0804CC98`, `0x0804D65C`,
`0x0804D76C`, `0x0804E5CC`, `0x0804E728`, `0x08058804`, `0x08058D54`,
`0x08059B48`, `0x08059C0C` — which is where a breakpoint goes (see OPEN below).

**SOLVED by breakpoint (2026-09-18): the id is an ordinary u16 argument.**
The table base is loaded by 70 `ldr rX,[pc,#imm]` sites inside 68 small
accessor functions, every one of them the same idiom:

```
movs r0,r0,lsl #16      ; (r0 & 0xFFFF)
movs r0,r0,lsr #11      ; << 5, i.e. id * 0x20
ldr  r1,[pc,#..]        ; r1 = 0x0861CA5C
adds r0,r0,r1           ; base + id*0x20
ldrb r0,[r0]            ; read a record field
```

So **r0 on entry is the terrain id** and `record = 0x0861CA5C + id*0x20`, with
the modifiers at `+0x16`. Observed live: id 1 = the elevation-5 sample's
terrain, id 2 = the elevation-7 sample's.

Verified end to end, not just by inspection: with the cursor walked across
tiles, the last id the probe logged (`id=4` -> `-10,5,10,-5,-10,10`) matches
the panel in the final rendered frame position for position — orange -10,
red +5, green +10, blue -5, white -10, grey +10 — and the terrain icon changed
with it.

**This is enough to drive a second-screen modifier panel**: hook the accessors,
cache the last id, look up the record. The hook is observability-only and never
touches guest state. The accessors fire exactly when the game rebuilds the
panel, so a cached id is in sync with what is on screen by construction.

**Elevation: SOLVED 2026-09-25** — it is a per-cell grid at `0x02016440`; see
"Depth of field on the battle map" at the end of this file. The rest of this
paragraph is kept as the record of how it was NOT found: the coordinates used
here were never absolute, which is why no layout fitted.

**STILL OPEN (as of 2026-09-18): elevation and the terrain icon.** Both are
per-tile, not per-terrain-type, so neither is in the record. `r4`/`r5` at `0x0806F868` looked
like tile coordinates (they change as the cursor moves) but are 1..4, far too
small for a ~46-tile-wide map, so they are not absolute coordinates. Constant
EWRAM pointers `r6=0x0202AB8C` and `r7=0x0202A900` at `0x0807226A` are the best
remaining lead; no row-major `base + (y*W + x)*E` layout fits the observed
(coord, id) triples for either base at any element size or width up to 64.

### Reproducing the probe

`src/kol_terrain_probe.cpp`, entirely env-gated and never installed otherwise:

```sh
KOL_TERRAIN_PROBE=1 GBARECOMP_INPUT_REPLAY=cursor.txt \
  ./build/KnightOfLodisRecomp --rom totkol.gba --bios ... \
  --no-window --load-state states/H_terrain_info.state --frames 900
```

Two traps cost real time here and are worth knowing:

- **A parked save state never exercises the lookup.** The panel is composited
  once; the accessors do not run again while the game idles. The cursor has to
  move, which means driving input.
- **`GBARECOMP_INPUT_REPLAY` frames are absolute `ppu.frame_count()`, and the
  frame a state loads at VARIES BETWEEN RUNS** (49303 one run, 44354 another,
  depending on how much boot happens before the deferred load applies). A
  replay file written for one run's load frame silently does nothing on the
  next — it just runs out before the state is restored. Cover a wide band with
  a repeating pattern instead of targeting exact frames.

`g_runtime_bus_read_override` does **not** work for faking KEYINPUT: the
runtime writes key state into the IO page with `set_keyinput`, so guest reads
never reach that override. Use the replay file.

Four earlier searches failed before the breakpoint route worked, for reasons
worth recording:

1. *Elevation as a fixed-address byte.* **Zero** offsets in all 256 KB hold 5
   in the elevation-5 state and 7 in the elevation-7 state. It is per-tile, not
   a global — the same shape of problem as the selected-unit record, which was
   solved with a pointer.
2. *Current-tile pointer.* Dereferenced every EWRAM-range u32 in both states
   and checked each target for an elevation byte plus an index byte. Zero
   candidates.
3. *Index as a fixed-address byte,* using the resolved index set. Six
   candidates, none with plausible elevation nearby; the most promising was the
   high byte of an unrelated object pointer at `0x02028C38`.
4. *A pointer at `0x02029B80`* that tracked perfectly between the two states —
   it is **MP2K song data**, not terrain. A pointer moving by exactly one
   record stride is not evidence on its own.

Also do not assume two sampled terrains are adjacent records: the second
state's modifier pattern appears in **8** different records, so it was never
pinned by its values alone.

Note the enclosing-function mapping matters: taking "greatest function entry
below the literal" is WRONG, because a literal pool sits after the code of the
function that references it and other functions can be interleaved. Decode the
actual Thumb `ldr rX,[pc,#imm]` instructions and map those PCs instead — the
first attempt watched 66 functions and caught one irrelevant call.

### KNOWN WRONG / OPEN

- ~~**STR/INT/AGI are BASE values.**~~ SOLVED 2026-09-20. The *results* are
  indeed stored nowhere, but the *inputs* are all in the ROM item table:
  displayed stat = record base + the four items' `+0x13/+0x14/+0x15`. Rictor's
  "INT 33 base against 38 in-game" is the Bandanna's `+5`. This entry also told
  the next reader "**do not go looking for addresses**" for Move and the weapon
  figures — half right, and it cost time: the weapon figures are computable
  (melee ATK = `STR + max(weapon PHYS, class innate) * class weapon% / 100`),
  Move still is not.
- ~~**Class field NOT identified.**~~ SOLVED 2026-09-20: it is record `+0x50`,
  indexing the class table at `0x08615228`. None of the five candidate offsets
  listed here was it, and the search that produced them could not have found it
  — class entries pair up male/female, so two Soldiers legitimately hold
  different ids and any "group units by displayed class name" test rejects the
  right field. A read watch found it in one run.
- APK is **81 MB containing 44 MB** of files. It was 42 MB with identical
  contents before the save-state work. Unexplained alignment/padding; not
  investigated, does not affect correctness.
- Second-screen cost to frame rate is **unmeasured**.

same reasoning as the `.bmp` dumps):

A and C were the two known (unit -> class) pairs back when class was a hunt.
It is no longer: class is record `+0x50`. These states are still the handiest
fixtures for checking a decode against a window the game actually drew.

## 16:9 extended view (2026-09-18)

The battle map renders at a true 16:9 **284x160** — and at up to 480x160 —
with authentic terrain in the added margins, on desktop and on the Thor.
Every other screen tested pillarboxes to black. This is an **opt-in,
default-off enhancement** in the sense of `gbarecomp/ENHANCEMENTS.md` Rule 1:
nothing below runs at the default 240x160.

**Note the actual number.** 16:9 at the GBA's 160 lines is `160 * 16/9 =
284.4`, so **284x160**, which is only 22 extra columns per side. An earlier
pass in this session used 426, which is 8:3, not 16:9 — it survives as a
useful stress width, not as the target.

### What is game policy and what is framework

The shared PPU already had the whole wide-surface capability
(`ENHANCEMENTS.md` §3): `RunOptions::max_view_width`, `--view-width`, and
per-pixel margin hooks. **No framework code was changed for this.** What the
game owed it was scene policy — which layers may appear in the margins, and
on which screens — and that lives in `src/kol_widescreen.cpp`, shared by the
desktop (`src/main.cpp`) and Android (`android/app/jni/main_android.cpp`)
entry points so the two builds cannot drift.

### The two invariants, both verified

1. **The faithful path is untouched.** At 240x160 the three reference states
   render byte-identical BMPs before and after this work.
2. **Widening never alters the authentic image.** At 284x160 *and* 480x160 the
   centre 240x160 of every widened frame is byte-identical to the faithful
   240x160 render of the same state. Margins only ever add.

Both are cheap to re-check and should be re-checked after any change here —
see "Re-verifying" below.

### Scene policy

`is_battle_map()` classifies a frame from DISPCNT + the four BGxCNT registers,
which the runtime hands the game each frame through `extended_view_frame`:

| Clause | Battle map | Why it is load-bearing |
|---|---|---|
| `mode == 0` | yes | the intro logos run **mode 2** (affine); those pillarbox |
| all four BGs enabled | `dispcnt & 0x0F00` | title (BG0/1) and story text (BG0/1/2) fail here |
| no WIN0/WIN1/OBJWIN | `dispcnt & 0xE000 == 0` | margin window semantics are undefined |
| BG0/BG1 are 512x256 | size code 1 | the terrain layers |
| BG0/BG1 char base 0 | | **the status screen reuses the same screen blocks from char block 2** — this clause is the one that separates them |
| BG2/BG3 are 256x256 | size code 0 | the HUD layers |

Matching scenes expose **BG0|BG1 only** in the margins. Everything else fails
closed to black.

**BG2/BG3 must be suppressed in the margins, and that is the whole trick.**
A GBA tilemap wraps; past the authentic 240 columns that wrap is not scenery,
it is a second copy of whatever the layer holds. With all four layers exposed,
the battle HUD ("GUEST / Rictor / HP:172") drew a duplicate of itself into the
left margin — a 256px-wide tilemap wrapping at 256. `g_ws_bg_x_provider`
suppresses non-world layers outside the native 240 and touches nothing inside
it.

Observed scene signatures (`KOL_WS_PROBE=1`), all from real runs:

| Scene | DISPCNT | BG0/1/2/3 | Classified |
|---|---|---|---|
| Battle map | `1F40` | `4C02/4E01/0B08/0A08` | **widen** |
| Battle preparation | `5F40` | `4C02/4E01/0B08/0A08` | **widen** |
| Battle preparation, back from Organize | `DF40` | `4C02/4E01/0B08/0A08` | **widen** (OBJWIN on but empty) |
| BATTLE START banner, first frame | `1B40` | `4C02/4E01/0B08/0A08` | **widen** (BG2 off, coming from the battle map) |
| BATTLE START banner | `9F40` | `4C02/4E01/0B08/0A08` | **widen** (OBJWIN gates only BG2, WINOUT `3F3B`) |
| Spell effect (Ice Javelin) | `1341`/`1741` | `4C02/4E01/4A0C/0B08` | **widen** (mode 1, coming from the battle map) |
| After the effect, camera back | `1340` | `4C02/4E01/4A08/0B08` | **widen** (BG2 512 wide but off) |
| Status screen | `1F40` | `6E0B/6C0A/2B09/2A09` | pillarbox |
| Title screen | `1360` | `990B/9B08/001F/001F` | pillarbox |
| Story intro | `1760` | `1D03/1E02/1F01/001F` | pillarbox |
| Intro logos | `1002`/`9802` | mode 2, affine | pillarbox |

**A window does not disqualify the battle map.** Battle preparation — the
deployment phase — is the same screen with WIN1 clipping the NAVI dialogue:
`5F40` against `1F40`, every BGxCNT identical. The classifier used to reject
anything with `dispcnt & 0xE000`, so the whole deployment phase pillarboxed.
Only OBJWIN disqualifies now; it is a per-pixel stencil built in 240-space with
no defined continuation past the native edge. **Refined 2026-09-25:** only
when a live sprite actually draws into it (OBJ mode 2). Coming back from
ORGANIZE, the game leaves the enable bit set (`DF40`) with no such sprite. The
deployment phase then stayed pillarboxed at 240x160 until the next scene
change (`states/BI_organize_return.state`: A on Organize, B, B). An empty OBJ
window selects nothing: every pixel is outside every window, which is how
margin columns are evaluated anyway. `KOL_WS_OBJWIN_STRICT=1` restores the
old rule. The rest of the signature (mode 0,
four BGs, BG0/BG1 512x256 out of char block 0, BG2/BG3 256x256) is what
identifies the scene, and the status screen stays separated by its char base.

**The BATTLE START banner keeps the wide view and the perspective
(2026-10-12).** After "Start battle? Yes", the game turns BG2 off for one
frame (`1B40`), then turns it back on with the OBJ window enabled (`9F40`).
WINOUT is `3F3B`, so BG2 (the words) shows only inside the banner's
OBJ-window sprites, as a wipe, and BLDCNT `3B44` fades it over the terrain.
Both frames failed the classifier, so for the ~165 frames of the banner the
view went back to 240x160 with no perspective, then widened again: the
camera seemed to jump twice (`states/GB_slot2_battle_start_camera.state`,
the user's slot 2: A on Yes at frame 2360; the banner runs 2464-2628).
There are two fixes:
- An OBJ window no longer disqualifies the scene when BG0, BG1 and OBJ are
  the same in its byte of WINOUT as in the outside byte. Then the window
  gates only the HUD layers, which are suppressed in the margins anyway.
- A frame with BG0|BG1 on and a HUD layer off stays the battle map if the
  previous frame was one. That is sticky only, so no new scene can start
  as a battle map this way.

`KOL_WS_PROBE` lines now also carry WININ/WINOUT.

**A spell's effect keeps them too (2026-10-12).** Ice Javelin in
`states/GD_slot3_spell_cast.state` (the user's slot 3, A on Cast at frame
12): the game turns BG2|BG3 off (176), then switches to **mode 1** with the
effect on an affine BG2 (`1341`/`1741`, BLDCNT `3344`, 338-440), then back
to mode 0 with BG2 off but still set up as the effect left it (`4A08`, 512
wide) while the camera pans back (440-683). Mode 1 and the 512-wide BG2
both failed the classifier, so the view dropped to 240x160 and flat for
~6 s. Now, coming from the battle map (sticky only): mode 1 is accepted
with BG0/BG1 still the terrain's, and BG2/BG3's sizes count only for a
layer that is drawn in mode 0. The effect (BG2) stays out of the margins
and draws flat over the warped scene, as the HUD does; the crystal is a
sprite and lands on its unit.

That alone left a **black band across both margins** for the height of the
dialogue. The PPU fails closed for margin rows whose 240 native pixels do not
all select the same window control (`gba_ppu.cpp`, "a guest-authored window has
no defined continuation beyond the native 240-pixel scanline"), which is every
row of a NAVI box. `g_ws_authored_margin_layers` is the framework's existing
opt-out, and KoL now sets it — but only once `map_source_tick()` has verified
the composed map against the guest's own drawn cells THIS frame, so the claim
rests on evidence rather than on the scene profile. Margin columns then
evaluate as outside the guest's window rectangles, with WINOUT governing them,
which is what "off the side of the native screen" means. A scene that merely
resembles the battle map cannot verify, does not get the claim, and stays
covered by the fail-closed rule.

OBJ is deliberately **not** clipped to the native viewport: a unit standing
past the old edge should be visible. In the verified battle state that is 38
pixels of one unit at the top-right and no parked-sprite junk.
`KOL_WS_OBJ_CLIP=1` forces the conservative clip if a later scene needs it.

### Running it

```sh
# desktop
./build/KnightOfLodisRecomp --rom totkol.gba --bios ../gbarecomp/bios/gba_bios.bin \
    --view-width 284
```

Android has no CLI, so it reads a marker file; **absent means faithful
240x160**, which is the default:

```sh
# "auto" picks the widest view that still scales by a WHOLE number.
# Or write an explicit width (284, 320, 480...).
adb shell "run-as com.koldecomp.game sh -c 'echo auto > files/widescreen.cfg'"
adb shell "run-as com.koldecomp.game sh -c 'rm files/widescreen.cfg'"   # back to 3:2
```

On Android the width is also switchable while playing, from the BACK menu's
Width list — see "The enhancement menu". `widescreen.cfg` still decides what
the view starts at.

**`auto` snaps to an integer scale, not to the exact aspect.** It takes the
largest integer scale whose 160 lines fit the panel, then the width that fills
it. On 1920x1080 that is 6x -> **320x160**, presented as 1920x960 with 60px
bars. Confirmed on the Thor:

```
android: display 1920x1080 -> integer scale 6x -> logical view 320x160 (1920x960, 60px bars)
```

Exact 16:9 at 160 lines is 284.4, which needs a **fractional 6.75x** scale: it
fills the height but scales unevenly, so some guest pixels come out larger than
others. 320 scales every guest pixel to exactly 6x6 device pixels and shows a
third more battlefield. The rule generalises — a 1280x720 panel also lands on
320. Widths above the integer-scale pick trade screen height for battlefield:

| Width | Scale | Image on 1920x1080 | Bars | Height used | Battlefield |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 284 | 6.75 (fractional) | 1920x1080 | none | 100% | +18% |
| **320** | **6 (integer)** | **1920x960** | **60px** | **89%** | **+33%** |
| 384 | 5 (integer) | 1920x800 | 140px | 74% | +60% |
| 480 | 4 (integer) | 1920x640 | 220px | 59% | +100% |

Diagnostics: `KOL_WS_PROBE=1` logs one line per scene-profile change with its
classification; `KOL_WS_FORCE_EXPOSE=1` ignores the policy and shows every
layer in the margins, which is how you find out whether a new scene's margins
hold real scenery or wrapped garbage.

### Continuing the bottom unit bar

The bar the game draws along the bottom when a unit is selected **is**
continued into the margins, seamlessly, rather than clipped. It is the one UI
element whose shape allows it: a full-bleed horizontal band with **no
decorative end caps** — a dark rule, a white highlight, a shaded rule, then a
cream field carrying an 8x8 tiled diagonal hatch.

Measured on `states/D_thor_unit_bar.state`:

- the band is screen `y 139..159`;
- rows 139/140/141 are each a single colour across all 240 columns;
- screen columns `0..7` are plain field — no glyphs — for every row of the band;
- the hatch is 8-periodic horizontally **and** vertically.

So the continuation is exact, not approximate: a margin column samples the
plain-field column with the same 8-pixel phase, `hw_x = hx mod 8`. Verified
numerically — across both seams `col(x) == col(x+8)` holds for every column of
the band, and rows 139-141 stay single-coloured across the full widened width.
Nothing is stretched, smeared or invented; it is the game's own tile pattern
continued in phase.

**It degrades safely with no "is the bar visible" test.** When no unit is
selected the bar is not drawn, so the source columns are transparent and the
margins keep showing terrain. Confirmed: `B_rictor_highlighted_map`, which has
a bottom-*right* corner panel instead of a full-width bar, renders
byte-identically at 284 with and without this rule.

`KOL_WS_NO_BAR=1` reverts to clipping for an A/B.

**The other HUD elements are still clipped**, and deliberately so — they are a
different shape. The top-left HP/MP bars are left-anchored and the top-right
info panel is right-anchored; both are finite panels with real edges, so
continuing them is meaningless. Making those reach the screen edges means
*shifting* them outward, not extending them, which is a different mechanism
(`out_hw_x` can do it) and changes where the game's own UI sits. Not attempted.

#### The opening's letterbox bars, edge to edge (2026-10-15)

Reported on the Thor (state GX = the user's slot 1, the opening's harbour
scene at 480x270): the black bars over and under the scene stopped at the old
240 edges, with the map showing past both ends. They are BG3 tiles on a scene
classified as the battle map (no window; DISPCNT `1F40`): row 0 at the top,
rows 16..19 at the bottom with the narration on BG2 from column 3. HUD
anchoring had already moved them to the view's top and bottom edges, but the
bar band above only continues the unit bar's measured rows 139..159, so the
top bar was not continued at all and the bottom one only below 139.

Now every **plain edge row** is continued whole (`g_plain_row`,
`plain_row_source` in kol_widescreen.cpp): a run of rows touching the top or
bottom edge where BG3 has all 30 columns drawn and its tiles at columns 0, 1
and 29 are the same entry, and BG2 has either nothing at column 0 or the same
test. The continuation samples columns 0..7 at the row's own scanline (after
its vertical anchoring), so a row passing the test repeats with no seam; a
framed box fails it (its end tiles are corner pieces) and is never smeared.
Gated with the bar (`KOL_WS_NO_BAR=1` turns both off).

Verified: GX at 480x270 frames 4 and 700 (narration up) bars full width;
byte-identical before/after at 480x270 on D_thor_unit_bar, B_rictor,
AU, BK, AI_prep_vertical, EW_newgame_dialogue, GA; both invariants
(66e13ab2 / 9054c456). `KOL_WS_UI_DUMP=N` now prints the Nth rebuild's grid
(1 = the first, as before).

### Margin contiguity: off-camera tilemap content

**The margins always show off-camera tilemap content.** BG0's tilemap is wider
than the camera — in `states/E_water_tile_margin.state`, `hofs=24` puts the
camera on tile columns 3..32 while the map itself occupies 0..45. Usually that
off-camera content IS the real map, which is why widening looks right. But the
tilemap also retains regions the game never displays from the current camera
position, and those render as scenery floating in the sky.

Found by playtesting on the Thor, not by the test suite. In state E, BG0 tile
column 35, rows 21..23 holds real tile indices (233, 208, 209, 112, 113) —
a fragment of water disconnected from the map, about 6x21 px at the extreme
right edge. It is **not** a 512-column tilemap wrap (the margin reads columns
264..285, well inside 512) and **not** uninitialised garbage.

An earlier revision of this file called the 480-wide stress test "strong
evidence" the margins were safe. That was wrong, and is corrected here: it was
one map whose off-camera content happened to be coherent.

**Rule:** a margin tile is drawn only when the same tile row has content at the
window edge, so only scenery contiguous with what is actually on screen
continues outward. **This is now the FALLBACK path only** — see "The composed
map is in EWRAM" above; when that lookup is armed the margins come from the
guest's own composed map and this heuristic is skipped. Needs `runtime_vram_view()` (added to the framework
alongside the existing `runtime_ewram_view()`, same read-only contract) —
the tilemap cannot be inspected from the rendered pixels.

Measured across every reference state, counting margin tile rows disconnected
from the window edge:

| State | Disconnected rows | Effect of the rule |
|---|---|---|
| `B_rictor_highlighted_map` | 0 | byte-for-byte no-op |
| `D_thor_unit_bar` | 0 | byte-for-byte no-op |
| `E_water_tile_margin` | 3 (BG0 col 35) | 118 px removed, exactly the artifact |

It is a **heuristic and it fails closed**: a genuinely detached island just
off-screen would be suppressed too. That is the right direction here — better a
missing rock than an invented one. The principled alternative is to find the
battle map's true extent in guest memory and mask to it; that is a real
reverse-engineering task and was not attempted, and note it would *not* have
rejected this island, which sits inside the map's column range.

### HUD edge anchoring

The battle HUD is authored for a 240px screen, so at 284 its corner panels keep
their native position and float 22px in from the edge. Anchoring moves each HUD
element out to the edge it was designed to sit against: the character info
panel returns to the bottom-right corner, the HP/MP bars to the left edge, the
top-right info panel to the right edge.

**This is the one place anything moves pixels INSIDE the authentic 240.**
Everything else here only adds margin. That is why it has its own switch:
`KOL_WS_NO_HUD_ANCHOR=1` disables it, and **invariant 2 is verified with it
off** (see "Re-verifying"). Invariant 1 is unaffected either way — none of this
runs at 240.

**The decision is made per element, not per scanline.** A scanline-local
"is this run touching the edge" test tears elements apart: in
`states/D_thor_unit_bar.state` the top-left HP bar occupies tile columns 1..7
on one row and 0..9 on the next, which would shift one row and not the other.
Instead each UI layer's tilemap is segmented into 4-connected components once
per frame (via `runtime_vram_view()`), and every tile of a component gets the
same shift. Classification by bounding box: spanning nearly the full width =>
full-width furniture, no shift; otherwise the box centre picks an edge.

**The vertical rule has the width cap too (fixed 2026-09-26).** A short box at
the top or bottom edge moves up or down only if it is at most 10 tiles wide,
like the horizontal rule, or full width (the bottom unit bar). Without it the
13-wide ARMS window, which starts at row 1, rose into the top margin and left
its hand cursor and weapon icon, which are sprites, behind
(`states/BQ_weapon_window_high.state`, 384x216). Both invariants unchanged.

### Pinning must not erase what anchoring moved in

The pinned character panel blanks the rect the guest drew it in, because it now
lives at the bottom right. That blanking used to run BEFORE HUD anchoring and
erased **any** UI in those columns, not just the panel's own. On the battle
preparation screen the "L VIEWMODE" / "R COMMAND" hints anchor right, straight
into the rect the panel had just vacated, and all but their first two glyphs
were erased — on the device they read "L VI" and "R CO".

Two changes, both small: the anchored lookup skips any candidate that resolves
into the panel's source rect (those cells belong to the panel, which is drawn
at its target, so they must not come back at their source), and the source
blank moved to AFTER anchoring. The panel cannot reappear through anchoring, so
the ordering loses nothing and keeps whatever else lands there.

`KOL_WS_UI_DUMP=1` prints the per-cell anchoring decision — `.` empty, `=`
occupied and unshifted, `>` / `<` shifted — which is how this was found. The
text was marked `>` across all eight of its columns, so anchoring was doing its
job and something downstream was eating the result.

### Left-aligning the character selection panel (2026-09-20)

The battle-preparation roster is a full-height panel at native columns 0..10.
In the wide view it sat 40px in from the screen edge, with battlefield to its
left. Anchoring it needs two things, and only doing the first is worse than
doing neither.

**It is one tile too wide for the corner rule.** Corner furniture is capped at
10 tiles, measured (the HP/MP cluster is 10x4, the terrain box 7x9), and the
roster is 11x20. The cap exists to keep cutscene frames and the ARMS box out,
and every one of those is a SHORT box — none more than about half the screen
tall — so a full-height component touching a screen edge anchors even at 11 or
12 wide. Width is still bounded: with a NAVI dialogue overlapping the roster,
the two merge into one 29-wide component on BG3 and must NOT be dragged to the
edge together.

**The portraits are OBJ sprites, and no BG provider moves sprites.** Anchoring
the frame alone slid it out from under its own contents — empty slots at the
edge, characters left floating over the map — which is exactly how the ARMS box
broke. OAM for `states/AD_user_charsel.state` has 14 active sprites in the
panel's columns: eight portrait halves (x=16 and 56, two sprites per character)
and four selection brackets (tile 287). They move with the panel through
`g_ws_obj_attr_x_provider`, the framework's existing per-game OBJ placement hook
— no framework change. It is called only by the expanded renderer, so the
faithful 240 path never sees it, and returning non-zero skips the hardware's
signed-X decode, so the hook does that decode itself.

**Units on the map are not the panel's (fixed 2026-09-25).** The rule moved
EVERY sprite whose X fell in the panel's native footprint (0..87), and the
battle-preparation deployment tiles lie partly there. Units placed on them
were carried behind the anchored panel. They were hidden at 240 too, under
the panel itself, so only the widened view showed the difference. Reported
as Alphonse and Lechies being on the field but not visible
(`states/BD_units_invisible.state`, 480x270). A sprite that matches a unit
the guest recorded in its world slot list (`obj_true_x`, kol_obj_cull.cpp)
now keeps its true X first; only the rest of the footprint travels with the
panel. The portraits are not in that list: `AD_user_charsel` at 480x270
renders byte-identical before and after. Both invariants are unchanged.

**Flashes on view mode (fixed 2026-09-25).** Pressing view mode (GBA L)
slides the panel out and back in over about four frames: its width goes
88 → 56 → 32 → 8 → gone, and back 32 → 56 → 80 → 88. There were two
flashes.
- **Portraits over the map.** Mid-slide, the game draws the portraits it has
  pushed off its own screen at NEGATIVE X, invisible at 240. They were left
  of the footprint, so they were not moved, and the widened view drew them
  in the left margin over the map for a frame or two. A panel anchored at
  the left edge (`x0 <= 0`) now owns everything left of its right edge too.
  Recorded world units are excluded first, as above.
- **A flash in the margins.** On the toggle frame the composed-map source
  fell back for one frame; see "A still camera keeps the margins" in the
  composed-map section.

Repro: `states/BD_units_invisible.state` at 480x270, with L at +37 and +137
frames after load (`GBARECOMP_INPUT_REPLAY` 172240/172340, `0x1FF`).

**Known limit:** while a NAVI dialogue overlaps the roster the merged component
is too wide to anchor, so the panel sits at its native position and snaps 40px
when the dialogue opens or closes. Separating them is not available — the
dialogue is drawn OVER the panel, and panel, bar and dialogue frames share one
9-slice tileset and palette bank, so neither components nor tile identity can
split them.

`KOL_WS_UI_DUMP=1` reports the resolved side panel: `side panel hw 0..87 shift
-40` on the roster, `0..-1 shift 0` on a battle map, where the rule must never
fire.

### Corner furniture is AT a corner, and takes its contents with it

Anchoring classified corner furniture by WIDTH alone — at most 10 tiles — and
then picked an edge from the bounding-box centre. That dragged things the game
places in WORLD space: the CHECK menu's Yes/No box sits at columns 11..16 in
the middle of the screen and was moved 40px left, away from its own hand
cursor, which is an OBJ sprite and does not move with it. Reported from the
device as the hand arrow not lining up with the text box.

A component must now also TOUCH a screen edge to anchor. Every real corner
element does by construction: the HP/MP cluster reaches column 0, the terrain
box and the info panel both end at column 29.

That alone un-anchored the HP/MP cluster, because **contents fail the edge test
even when their container passes it**: the HP/MP figures on BG2 start three
columns inside the BG3 frame that holds them. They stayed put, and the existing
"anything drawn on a component that is staying put stays put with it" pass then
dragged the frame back to match, un-anchoring the cluster (4,856 pixels against
the previous build). So a container's shift now propagates to its contents
first, bounded by CONTAINMENT — a shift reaches only what is drawn inside the
moving element — and the stay-put pass runs after it.

Consequence worth knowing: the battle-preparation hints "L VIEWMODE" /
"R COMMAND" (BG2 columns 12..19, touching no edge) now stay at their native
centre position instead of being anchored right. They are button legends, not
corner furniture.

### Furniture is found WITHOUT connected components

The unit panel and the bottom bar are found by scanning the tile grid, not by
segmenting it. Components merge whatever touches, and the panel's bottom row
sits on the bar's top row — so the two became one component and neither matched
its shape: no pin, and no bar to continue. Three symptoms, one cause.

Tile identity cannot rescue this the way it did the terrain box: the panel, the
bar and cutscene dialogues are drawn from the **same 9-slice tileset in the
same palette bank** (fill `0x01-0x08`, borders `0x19-0x20`, bank 4). Both were
checked before settling on grid scans.

- **Bar:** a run of rows ending at the bottom with at least 26 of 30 columns
  occupied on BG3, the run being **at most 4 rows**. The length limit matters:
  a bottom-anchored dialogue measured 27 wide over rows 15..19 and would
  otherwise be "continued" into the margins.
- **Panel:** a solid 10x7 block on BG3 whose interior carries the `HP:` and
  `MP:` label tiles on BG2. Solidity alone is not enough — a dialogue box
  contains many 10x7 solid sub-rectangles — and the labels are what make it the
  unit panel. Verified: found in all five states that have one, and in none of
  the seven that do not.
- **Pin target:** bottom-right, but **above the bar** when one is up. Pinning to
  the screen bottom regardless dropped the panel onto the bar and buried its MOV
  readout; the game itself puts the panel above it.

**Only corner-sized components anchor, bounded by measurement.** The cutoff is
10 tiles, which is exactly the width of the widest real corner furniture — the
HP/MP cluster is 10x4 and the terrain box 7x9 — rather than a margin above it.
Everything that broke was wider: a 22-wide cutscene frame, its 14-wide caption,
and a 13-wide ARMS box.

The ARMS box is the instructive one. Its weapon and shield icons are **OBJ
sprites** (confirmed in OAM), and sprites are not touched by any of these BG
providers, so anchoring slid the box out from under its own icons. Anything
whose content is partly sprites cannot be moved by this mechanism at all.

**Bar continuation requires a real bar.** It used to fire on
`screen_y >= kBarTopY` alone. The dialogue box occupies the same scanlines, so
continuing *it* painted repeated vertical slices of the box across the rest of
the band. It now also requires full-width furniture to actually exist this
frame.

**And "full-width furniture" means the bar, not a wide box.** A first fix
tested width `>= 27` of 30, which a 27x8 dialogue satisfied — so continuation
re-enabled and smeared slices into both margins instead. The test is now the
full 30 columns *and* at most 4 rows tall. Measured: the real bottom bar is
30x3; the two dialogues seen are 25x8 and 27x8, so both clauses matter and
neither is tight.

**Contents inherit their container's non-shift.** A dialogue's text lives on
one layer *inside* its frame on the other, and the two are independent
components. One cutscene box measured 22 columns wide — left alone — with
14-wide text, which passed the corner test and anchored right, sliding the last
word out of its own frame. Any component drawn over a component that is staying
put now stays put with it. This generalises the full-width rule below, which
was the same failure with the bottom bar.

**Bar content stays put, deliberately.** The bottom unit bar's background is
full-width on BG3 while its labels and figures live on BG2. Shifting those
independently separated the bar's frame from its contents — it drew a stray box
outline around the "A" of "Alphonse". Anything sharing a tile row with
full-width furniture is treated as bar content and is not anchored; only
free-standing corner panels move. The bar still spans the full width through
the continuation rule above.

Verified on `F_char_info_panel.state` and `B_rictor_highlighted_map.state`:
the panel's opaque body is a **pixel-exact translation** of the native panel by
`extra_left + extra_right`. The only differing pixels are its 1-2px dithered
border (and one 1px transparent column at x=237), where the terrain showing
through is now different terrain — because terrain does not move. That is
correct, not distortion.

### Pinning the character info panel

The guest moves the unit info panel around the screen so it does not cover the
selected sprite. It is **not** a left/right corner swap — it relocates in both
axes: `states/F_char_info_panel.state` has it at tile cols 20..29 rows 13..19,
`states/G_panel_left.state` at cols 10..19 rows 6..12. Widescreen gives the
panel a permanent home, so it is pinned flush to the bottom-right of the wide
view and the guest's avoidance placement is overridden.

**Identified structurally, not by position:** the panel is the only **solid
10x7 tile block on BG3**. Verified across every battle state — F, G and B each
have exactly one such component, at three different positions, and D (which
shows the bottom bar instead) has none; its components are 10x4 ragged, 7x9
ragged, and the 30x3 full-width bar. Both the BG3 background and the BG2
contents move by the same delta, and the source rectangle is blanked.

Relocating in Y needed a second framework seam: `g_ws_bg_y_provider`, the
vertical companion to the existing `g_ws_bg_x_provider`, supplying a substitute
source scanline for a regular-BG sample. Its layer mask defaults to 0, so games
that do not use it pay nothing. `g_ws_bg_tilemap_provider` could not do this —
it is only consulted for margin columns (`sample_hx < 0 || >= 240`), and the
panel moves inside the native area.

Verified as a **pure translation**: at both 284 and 480 the panel interior is
pixel-exact against the native panel; only the 4px dithered border differs,
where the terrain behind it is now different terrain. `F` (already bottom-right)
and `D` (no panel) render byte-identically with pinning on or off.

`KOL_WS_NO_PANEL_PIN=1` restores the guest's own placement.

**Left out while the second screen shows the unit (2026-09-28).** The user's
call: with the Thor's second screen up, the box repeats it. It is then
vacated exactly as pinning vacates it and drawn nowhere (`g_panel_hide`).
"Up" means both of these:
- the "Second screen panel" setting is on;
- the Android thread finds the presentation display
  (`SecondScreen.available()`, polled with the stats push).

Switching the setting off brings the box back at once. The desktop has no
second screen and keeps it. `KOL_HIDE_UNIT_PANEL=1` forces it off for desktop
tests, `KOL_NO_HIDE_UNIT_PANEL=1` keeps it. Checked on `F_char_info_panel` and
`G_panel_left` at 480x270, with and without the perspective: only the pinned
box's own 80x56 changes. Both render invariants are unchanged.

**SP: as well as MP:.** Some units' box reads SP: (tiles `0xAC/0xAD`) where
most read MP: (`0xAA/0xAB`). Found with `states/CC_box_elsewhere1.state`
(Basac, "SP:150") and `CD_box_elsewhere3.state` (Vector, "SP:111"). The
panel test only knew MP:, so those boxes were never recognised: not pinned,
not left out, and left wherever the game had put them. Either label now
counts.

**Which units have SP (2026-09-28).** The game decides it per class, the
same way in the map box (`0x0801ED9A`, found with a write watch on the box's
tilemap copy at `0x02028A78` in `CC_box_elsewhere1`) and in the status window
(`0x0806EF28`). It reads class field `0x0F` through the accessor
`0x0813FA44` (u16 class `+0x18`, with the usual `+0x09` fallback). With bit
`0x80` set, the second gauge is SP. That is 71 classes (Griffin, Hawkman, …).
The figures are the record's MP fields either way.
- Label: `0xAC/0xAD` in bank `+0x5A` high nibble of `0x086B7530` (12,
  green), instead of `0xAA/0xAB` in `+0x59` (13, pink).
- Bar (`0x0806EBD0` mode 2): caps `0xC8`, fill `0xC9-0xCD`, each in its own
  bank, instead of `0xC2-0xC7`.

Checked on six units: Basac and Vector SP; Orson, Brigitte, Rictor and
Alberich MP, as each game box shows. The second screen's sheet
(`UnitInfo::sp`, `kol_sheet.cpp`) now draws SP the same way. The accessor's
jump table starts at `0x0813FA78` (the word at `0x0813FA74` is its address),
so field `0x0F` is `+0x18`; reading it one entry early gave `+0x17` and the
wrong answer.

### Cost

**The table that used to be here was wrong, and wrong in a way worth
remembering.** It reported 240 = 83.5 fps, 284 = 80.6, 426 = 77.9 and concluded
"the PPU is not the bottleneck." It timed whole headless runs, and on macOS
startup is ~21 s of `dlopen` for 1554 warm self-heal overlays. That constant
swamped the per-frame difference and turned a +52% cost into an apparent +7%.

Measure steady state by **differencing two frame counts** so startup drops out,
and set `GBARECOMP_SELFHEAL_RECOMPILE=0` (that tier is off on Android anyway,
and it changes steady-state cost by nothing — 6.62 vs 6.67 ms/frame — it only
buys startup time):

```sh
for n in 200 800; do time ./build/KnightOfLodisRecomp ... --frames $n; done
# ms/frame = (t800 - t200) / 600
```

macOS, `states/S_move_highlight.state`, before and after the IWRAM work below:

| view | before | after | |
|---|---|---|---|
| 240x160 | 6.60 ms/frame | **4.21** | −36% |
| 480x160 | 10.00 ms/frame | **7.61** | −24% |
| 480x270 | 10.03 ms/frame | **7.59** | −24% |

**The 480x270 row above is really 480x160 — see the next paragraph.**

**Headless runs never applied the height (found 2026-09-23).** `KOL_VIEW_SIZE`
asks through `runtime_request_view_size`, which is applied only at a boundary a
headless run never reaches until EXIT (the request lands 0.12 s in, the log
says `NOT APPLIED` at 6.03 s, which is the end). So every desktop "480x270"
number, including the table above and the "height is free" paragraph below,
rendered 160 rows and only the final dump at 270. The Thor renders all 270
every frame. Make a desktop run really 270 tall with
`GBARECOMP_VIEW_EXTRA_Y=55` (applied at startup) alongside `KOL_VIEW_SIZE`.
Startup is ~0.3 s now, not 21 s.

Measured properly (f50fce1, `S_move_highlight`): 240 **4.06**, 480x160
**7.42**, 480x270 **11.34** ms/frame. The height costs MORE than the width.
After the 2026-09-23 work (fast-forward render skip, HUD anchoring by row,
lean compositor candidates), `AU_thor_battle_perf` at a real 480x270:
**11.03 -> 6.99** ms/frame at 1x, and **3.98** per guest frame at 4x
fast-forward (1 frame in 4 composed) — about a plain 240 frame (3.89).
On the Thor, 4x fast-forward went **1.28x -> 2.67x** from the render skip
alone; 1x unchanged at 59.5 fps, ~85% of a core.

**WRONG — see above: height was never applied headlessly.** Width is expensive; height is free. +240 columns costs +3.4 ms, +110 rows
costs 0.03 ms. The cost is therefore NOT per-pixel — do not model it that way.
Crossing from `render_scanline_internal` to `render_scanline_wide` at all is
what costs. The vertical expansion is not part of this problem.

On-device (AYN Thor, 480x270, battle map), measured 2026-09-22 with no rebuild:

- **fps**: `adb shell dumpsys SurfaceFlinger --latency "'<layer>'"`, layer name
  from `--list` — the `(BLAST)` SurfaceView, quoted twice (shell + adb). Diff
  the middle column. Result: **59.1 fps**, median gap 16.66 ms.
- **CPU**: the guest thread is `Thread-4`; read `$14+$15` of
  `/proc/<pid>/task/<tid>/stat` against `/proc/uptime`. Result: **99.0% of one
  core**.

`dumpsys gfxinfo` measures the HWUI second-screen panel, NOT the emulator
surface — do not read it as the game's frame rate.

99% of a core at 59 fps is zero headroom, and it is the whole explanation for
both reports, that 480 ran poorly and that fast-forward barely did anything: fast-forward
runs N guest frames per presented frame and there is no spare CPU to run them.

### KNOWN WRONG / OPEN

- **Still only a handful of camera positions.** The contiguity rule above was
  derived from the one artifact found so far and verified against four states.
  It bounds the failure mode; it does not prove the margins are right in
  general. **Keep checking new maps, mid-scroll and immediately after a map
  load.** Less load-bearing now that the margins read the composed map, which
  is checked against the guest's own drawn cells every frame — but the
  composed-map path itself is verified on twelve states of two battles, which
  is not the whole game either.
- **The composed map's bounds are inferred, not read.** 128 columns comes from
  the blit's own `0..0x7F` range check and its `0x100` row stride; 96 rows
  comes from BG1's array sitting `0x6000` later. A map taller than 96 rows
  would need that re-derived, and would show up as the wrap search failing
  (margins fall back, `map_source:` logs it) rather than as wrong scenery.
- **The array pointer is read from a fixed address** (`0x02026CA8`), seen with
  the same value in two different battles. If a battle ever allocates it
  elsewhere the per-frame check fails closed. The way to check is `KOL_WS_FORCE_EXPOSE=1` plus a look at the
  margins, and a save state committed to `states/` when something looks wrong.
- **Pinning overrides collision avoidance the guest does for a reason.** The
  guest moves the panel to keep it off the selected sprite; pinned, it can
  cover a unit standing in the bottom-right of the wide view. 16:9 makes that
  rarer, not impossible — a unit near the right edge of the map can still end
  up behind it. Accepted deliberately; `KOL_WS_NO_PANEL_PIN=1` reverts.
- **The 10x7 panel signature is from four states.** A larger or smaller info
  panel (a different unit type, a status effect list) would not match and would
  simply not be pinned, which fails closed.
- **HUD anchoring and panel pinning move pixels inside the authentic 240.** By
  design, and the only features here that do. It is classified from tilemap occupancy, so an
  element whose tiles are non-empty but whose pixels are fully transparent
  would still be treated as content. Verified only on the battle map.
- **The full-width threshold and the left/right split are both tuned to this
  HUD** (a component spanning >= 27 of 30 tile columns is furniture; the
  bounding-box centre picks the edge). A battle screen with a differently
  proportioned HUD could classify wrongly. Check new screens with
  `KOL_WS_NO_HUD_ANCHOR=1` for an A/B.
- **The bar band is a hardcoded `y >= 139`.** It was measured from one state.
  If any battle screen draws a different full-width band at a different height,
  this rule will not find it, and if some other scene puts content in BG2/BG3
  columns 0..7 below y=139 it would be replicated into the margins. Only the
  battle map reaches the rule at all, which bounds the blast radius.
- ~~The runtime's `extended view ON:` banner never appears on Android.~~
  **RESOLVED — it was never a mystery: `--window` sets `quiet`**
  (`gbarecomp/src/runtime/runtime.cpp`, in the `--window` arm of the argument
  parser), and the Android entry point always passes `--window`. So every
  windowed session suppresses that banner on every platform, not just Android.
  Reproduced on macOS. Not a behaviour bug; note it before gating any new
  player-facing message on `!args.quiet`, because on a handheld every session
  is windowed. The save-state combos print ungated for exactly this reason.
- **The world map cannot be extended on EITHER axis, and a pillarboxed scene
  now drops to the authentic surface.** Vertically measured 2026-09-21 on
  `states/AM_worldmap_vertical.state`: all four BG layers stop at tile row 19.

  | layer | non-empty rows | cols |
  |---|---|---|
  | BG0 | 0..19 of 32 | 0..29 |
  | BG1 | 0..19 of 32 | 0..31 |
  | BG2 | 12..18 | 5..26 |
  | BG3 | 0..19 of 32 | 0..31 |

  There is no taller artwork and, unlike a battle map, no composed array in
  EWRAM holding more — the guest never builds one for this scene.

  What that exposed is worth more than the answer. A pillarboxed scene at a
  wider view is drawn SMALLER: at 480x270 the world map still occupies 240x160
  of the surface, so a 1920x1080 panel shows it at 4x = 960x640, against 6.75x
  = 1620x1080 when the surface is 240x160 itself. Picking a wider view shrank
  every non-battle scene to under a third of the panel. The scene policy now
  requests the authentic size when a scene has no margin content and the
  chosen size when it does — measured on the Thor at 84% of the panel against
  30% before, switching both ways as states are loaded. Inert unless a
  player-facing size exists, so the desktop runner still honours
  `--view-width` exactly.

  **WHEN it resizes matters as much as whether.** The first version debounced
  30 frames against a classifier flicker I had assumed rather than measured,
  and that put the resize half a second AFTER the new scene was already on
  screen — which is exactly what it looked like. `is_battle_map()` is a pure
  function of DISPCNT and the four BGxCNTs, so it flips the moment the game
  writes the incoming scene's registers, before the scene fades in; acting
  then puts the resize inside the transition where it cannot be seen. The gate
  is the display state rather than a timer now: hold while DISPCNT has FORCED
  BLANK set, because a blanked frame is a scene being torn down and its
  registers mean nothing, and otherwise act on two consecutive agreeing
  frames. Six scene loads on the Thor produced five resize requests, one per
  genuine change, with no oscillation.
- **The world map CANNOT be widened, and that is now measured, not assumed.**
  Its BG0 is `2F03` — size code 0, a 256x256 tilemap, i.e. 32 tile columns for
  a 30-column screen. That leaves exactly **two spare tile columns**; a 320
  view needs ten per side, so everything past them is the tilemap wrapping.
  `KOL_WS_FORCE_EXPOSE=1` on `states/AF_world_map.state` shows it plainly: a
  second WAR FUNDS plate and a second gryphon appear in the margins. There is
  no further artwork to reveal. Its two corner plates COULD be pushed out to
  the screen edges over the black bars (both are pure BG — of 128 active
  sprites only the four map markers are on screen, the rest parked at the
  x=248/y=168 idiom), but that spreads the HUD without gaining any map, and it
  was offered and declined 2026-09-20. Leave the scene pillarboxed.
- **Cutscenes, shops, and combat animations are untested** —
  they simply pillarbox today, which is correct-by-default but means the
  feature covers less of the game than "16:9 Knight of Lodis" suggests.
- Not exposed in the player-facing launcher (`launcher_expose_widescreen =
  false`) precisely because only one scene type is validated.
- No oracle diff was run against the widened path, and none is meaningful:
  mGBA has no 284x160 reference. The centre-240 byte-identity check above is
  the substitute, and it is a weaker claim.

### Every enhancement and its switch

Everything this project adds to the authentic presentation is reversible, and
each switch reverts one thing rather than the whole feature. All default to
ENABLED; setting the variable to 1 turns that enhancement off.

| enhancement | switch |
|---|---|
| the extended view itself | `files/widescreen.cfg` (absent = faithful 240), `--view-width` + `GBARECOMP_VIEW_EXTRA_Y`; on Android the BACK menu's **View size** list, whose first entry (240x160) is "off" |
| see-through blue movement tiles | `KOL_WS_NO_HIGHLIGHT_BLEND`; `KOL_HIGHLIGHT_ALPHA=0..16` tunes it |
| ...remembered per world cell, so it stays see-through while scrolling | `KOL_WS_NO_HIGHLIGHT_WORLD` (back to the ring-slot shadow) |
| margins drawn from the composed map | `KOL_WS_NO_MAP_SOURCE` (falls back to tilemap + contiguity) |
| HUD edge anchoring | `KOL_WS_NO_HUD_ANCHOR` |
| character info panel pinning | `KOL_WS_NO_PANEL_PIN` |
| bottom unit bar continuation | `KOL_WS_NO_BAR` |
| character selection panel left-aligned | `KOL_WS_NO_SIDE_PANEL` |
| widening windowed scenes (battle prep) | `KOL_WS_NO_WINDOWED_MAP` |
| OBJ beyond the native viewport | `KOL_WS_OBJ_CLIP` (clips it, the conservative rule) |
| depth of field on the battle map (**off** by default) | BACK menu "Depth of field (follows the cursor)"; desktop `KOL_EDGE_BLUR=1` forces it on, `KOL_NO_EDGE_BLUR=1` off; `KOL_NO_FOCUS=1` falls back to top/bottom bands; `KOL_EDGE_BLUR_HUD=1` blurs the HUD too |

**Correctness fixes deliberately have NO switch**, because turning them off does
not restore a different presentation, it restores a bug: the save-state
architectural-boundary guard (an unloadable state and a crash), the
pin-before-anchor ordering (erased button hints), the both-directions ring
search (mangled margins), and the edge test on corner furniture (a menu dragged
away from its own cursor). `KOL_WS_NO_HUD_ANCHOR` already covers anchoring as a
feature if it needs to come off wholesale.

**The second screen is the one gap.** It binds whenever an Android Presentation
exists and has no gate at all. An environment variable would not help there —
the second screen only exists on the handheld, where env vars are unreachable,
which is exactly why the extended view needed `widescreen.cfg`. Gating it
properly means a player-facing setting, not a developer knob.

### The enhancement menu (2026-09-20)

**A fresh install starts on Enhanced (2026-10-11).** With no
`files/enhancements.cfg`, `settings_init` takes the Enhanced preset (384x216,
perspective, depth of field Medium, AO Half tile (Full until 2026-10-21), shadows, torchlight, unit
shadows, lifted props and walls, clear move range, wide weather, fast
loading, water) before the hosts' own defaults are applied. A saved file
still wins, key by key. Only Android calls `settings_init`, so desktop runs
keep the switches' own defaults and the test recipes are unchanged.

**BACK opens it** on Android — `MainActivity.dispatchKeyEvent` intercepts
`KEYCODE_BACK` before SDL's surface sees it, and everything else still falls
through to the guest. The dialog is built from the NATIVE list
(`kol::Setting`), not a Java copy, so adding a toggle in `kol_settings.h` makes
it appear with no Java change. Choices apply immediately and persist in
`files/enhancements.cfg`.

Two toggles and a size list:

| item | what it covers |
|---|---|
| **View size** (button) | the whole extended view — width AND height — including margins, HUD anchoring, panel pinning, bar continuation, side-panel alignment and prep widening. `240x160` is the first entry, so it is also the off switch |
| See-through move range | the blue movement tiles |
| Second screen panel | the Thor's unit panel and terrain mirror |

**There is no Widescreen checkbox.** A checkbox beside a width list is two
controls for one thing that can disagree with each other — and "off" is just a
size. It is the first entry of the list now:

```
settings: view ladder (5): 240x160 284x160 320x180 *384x216 480x270
```

**Height travels with width, as one request.** A view widened at scale N wants
the matching height at scale N, and asking for them separately renders a frame
at the wrong aspect in between; `runtime_request_view_size()` carries both. On
a 1080p handheld each integer entry fills the panel exactly with no bars, so
the ladder says so rather than quoting a bar height. The height is never read
from `enhancements.cfg` — it is looked up from the ladder for the stored
width, so a config copied from another device cannot ask for a size this panel
cannot show.

The ladder is built natively (`kol_settings.cpp`, `build_width_ladder`) from
the panel the game is actually running on, by the same arithmetic
`widescreen.cfg=auto` uses — one entry per integer scale whose 160 lines fit,
plus 284 (true 16:9 at 160 lines). Each row names its trade-off, because the
player cannot be expected to know it: `320x180  6x, fills the screen`, and for
284, `no bars, uneven pixels`.

**284, not 285.** True 16:9 at 160 lines is 284.44. The framework's own
fixed-16:9 helper rounds up with `(160*16+8)/9`; the ladder floors instead,
both because 284 is the nearer integer and because rounding up would crop —
and because 284 is the width the second render invariant is recorded at, so
the menu and the reference agree.

**`auto` still picks 320 at launch.** The ladder only lets the player move
along it while playing; it does not change what the marker file resolves to.
Comparing 320 / 384 / 480 on the Thor at the same camera, 384 is where the
map stops being cropped at both edges and 480 spends most of its extra width
on empty sea, but that is a preference, which is why it is a menu item rather
than a new default.

**Widescreen needs no per-feature wiring.** It switches the view width between
the resolved width and 240, and at 240 the widened path is never consulted, so
every one of those enhancements goes inert by construction. That is what makes
one switch honest rather than a checklist someone has to maintain.

Live width changes go through the framework's `runtime_request_view_width()`,
serviced at a dispatch boundary — the same path the Widescreen toggle uses, so
the width list needed no new plumbing. Verified on the Thor: picking 384 mid-
battle logs `view width 384 -> 384 (margins 72/72)`, the panel goes to
1920x800 with 140px bars, the HUD re-anchors to the new edges and the margins
keep drawing real map with no fallback. Two things bit on the way, both worth
not re-learning:

- **The request needs a present unwind to be serviced at all.** With
  present-in-place a single `step_once()` spans many frames, so without one the
  toggle sat pending until some unrelated unwind happened.
- **Clear the unwind flag when servicing it.** The save path does; the first
  version of the width path did not, so every later `step_once()` returned
  immediately, the guest stopped advancing, and the screen went black and
  frozen while the process stayed alive.

The unwind itself is now gated in the framework on no-IRQ-nesting AND
User/System mode, which is what stopped it corrupting the guest — see the
gbarecomp commit; toggling on a battle map aborted at `pc=0x08BA1C02` before
that gate existed.

**The desktop has no menu.** recomp-ui is not vendored here, so `ui_extra_items`
has no consumer, there is no paint-over-frame seam, and the game cannot see host
key presses. Desktop keeps the environment variables. Giving it the same menu
means adding those seams to gbarecomp first.

**A player-facing menu is reachable without touching the framework.**
`RunOptions` carries `ui_extra_items` with `ui_get`/`ui_set`/`ui_action`/
`ui_enabled` — "game-owned items appended to the in-game settings menu", whose
documented rationale is that "the only alternative to a menu entry is not an
undocumented keystroke" (Boktai's light source is the precedent). Each gate
above is already a live per-frame read of a global, so a menu value would slot
in where `env_on()` sits today, with the env var kept as an override. View
width is the one item that reshapes the surface rather than only re-rendering,
so it needs its own validation before going in a menu.

### Vertical view expansion (2026-09-21)

The extended view can be taller than 160 lines, and on Android the height is
**part of the size choice** rather than a separate knob — see "The enhancement
menu". Desktop still asks for it explicitly, since it has no menu:

```sh
# desktop: rows per SIDE. 28 + --view-width 384 gives 384x216.
GBARECOMP_VIEW_EXTRA_Y=28 ./build/KnightOfLodisRecomp ... --view-width 384
```

**Why it was capped at 0, and why that reason does not bite here.** Horizontal
widening reuses each scanline's own latched register state; a margin ROW has
no scanline, so in general the compositor would have to invent one. Measured
over 10 frames of the battle map and of a cutscene, the only PPU register
writes this game makes are the VBlank forced-blank toggle — DISPCNT twice a
frame, DISPSTAT once. No BG scroll, no window, no blend, no affine change
mid-frame. HBlank IRQ is enabled on both and its handler touches no PPU
register. So margin rows borrow the nearest real line — top from line 0,
bottom from line 159 — and nothing is invented. Rows outside `[0,160)` resolve
to WINOUT and get no OBJ-window stencil, the same conservative rule the margin
columns use.

**The payoff, on the Thor**, and the reason the height belongs with the width
rather than beside it. Every ladder width has a height that fills the panel
exactly at its integer scale, and all three are exactly 16:9 with square
pixels:

| view | scale | on 1920x1080 | bars |
|---|---|---|---|
| 320x180 | 6x | 1920x1080 | none |
| **384x216** | **5x** | **1920x1080** | **none** |
| 480x270 | 4x | 1920x1080 | none |

Confirmed at 384x216: the top device row is the map's sky, the bottom is
water, and the letterbox colour `(8,11,19)` appears nowhere in the frame.

**Verified.** With the knob unset both render invariants are unchanged. With
it set, the centre 240x160 of a 384x216 frame is byte-identical to the
faithful 240 render — 0 of 160 rows differing, the vertical analogue of the
centre-240 identity check:

```sh
KOL_WS_NO_HUD_ANCHOR=1 KOL_WS_NO_PANEL_PIN=1 GBARECOMP_VIEW_EXTRA_Y=28 \
    ./build/KnightOfLodisRecomp ... --view-width 384 --dump-bmp out384x216.bmp
# crop 240x160 at x=72, y=28 and compare with out240.bmp
```

**Full-height side furniture continues into the margin.** The roster panel
otherwise keeps its authentic 160-line height with map above and below it,
which reads as the panel floating in a hole. How to continue it is measured
per frame, not assumed: the panel's background is a hatch periodic in BOTH
axes (on `AI_prep_vertical`, BG3 columns cycle tiles 005-008 and the rows
repeat every 2 tile rows), so the margin repeats that period, and only on the
layer the background sits on. `KOL_WS_NO_PANEL_EXTEND=1` turns it off.

Two things that were tried first and are wrong, so they are not re-tried:
repeating ONE scanline turns the diagonal hatch into vertical streaks, and
repeating the panel's top rows stamps slices of the portrait frames down the
margin — the portraits are on the other UI layer, which is why only the
background layer is continued.

**What is NOT done, and is why this is a probe:**
**A dialog box is no bar (fixed 2026-11-04).** "Full width" meant 30 tiles, for the bottom
unit bar, and a speaker's box drawn at the screen's left is exactly that: it went to the view's
top border (states/thor/0117, 28 rows up at 384x216), while the same box further right stayed
(states/thor/0113). A 30-wide component on BG3 with the box's frame tiles (0x19-0x20) in its top
row now stays where the game put it. `KOL_WS_WIDE_BOX_ANCHORED=1`: as before.

**The HUD anchors vertically too.** A short box drawn against the top or
bottom of the authentic 160 lines follows that edge out, by the same rule as
the horizontal one: bounded size, touches the edge, and a box touching neither
is in world space and stays. The bottom bar and everything sharing its rows go
together, and the bar's horizontal continuation follows it down.

Three things this needed that the horizontal side had already learned, and one
it had not:

- **A container takes its contents with it.** The HP/MP readout is several
  DISCONNECTED BG2 components at different tile rows inside one BG3 frame.
  Classified on their own, only the top row moved: `10 / 12` rendered as
  `0 / 2` with two stray 1s left at the old height. The vertical pass
  propagates a container's shift to what is drawn inside it, then a stay-put
  pass, exactly as the horizontal one does.
- **No OBJ hook is involved, and one was written before that was checked.**
  The HP/MP readout tearing as `0 / 2` looked like sprites left behind, so a
  vertical OBJ hook went in to carry them. It was never what fixed the tear —
  the containment pass above was — and matching sprites to a moved box by
  bounding rectangle then claimed WORLD sprites that merely overlapped it:
  units pinned to the top edge with the terrain they stand on scrolled away
  beneath them, reported at 480x270. Measured with the hook removed: the
  HP/MP readout, the MEMBER counter and the character info box all still move
  intact, because every glyph they carry is BG. The hook is gone from the
  framework too.

  The discriminator does not exist in the frame, which is why no smarter rect
  test would have worked: in `states/AN_obj_margin.state` the world units
  overlapping the HP/MP box and the box's own 8x8 glyph are all OBJ priority
  1, and some units sit FULLY inside the box's rectangle. Anything that moves
  HUD sprites here has to identify them some other way.
- **The height cap is 8 tile rows, not half the screen**, and anything inside
  the side panel's columns is excluded. The roster's right-hand portrait
  column is 10 rows tall starting at row 0, and a half-screen cap swept it up
  into the margin.
- **The edge test allows one tile of slack, on BOTH axes.** The character info
  box ends at row 18 with row 19 unused, and the battle-preparation MEMBER
  counter is drawn at columns 25..28 with column 29 unused — an exact test
  left each of them stranded while everything around them anchored. The slack
  cannot reach the world-space case the test exists to exclude: the CHECK
  menu's Yes/No box ends at column 16.

`KOL_WS_NO_HUD_ANCHOR=1` covers this as it does the horizontal anchoring.
**The margin tilemap provider had to learn about ROWS.** It was gated on
`sample_hx < 0 || sample_hx >= 240` — a margin COLUMN — which was complete
while the view could only widen. A margin ROW at a CENTRE column skipped it
and fell through to the wrapped 256px ring, the stale seam the provider exists
to replace, and that rendered as a flat band of sky cutting across the
picture.

**It was diagnosed wrong twice before it was diagnosed right, and the wrong
answer was the plausible one**: "the composed map has no data up there, the
battlefield is a diamond and this is its edge." Both times the evidence was
a dump too narrow to see past. The first looked at 12 columns at the screen's
left edge, where the diamond genuinely is empty. The second scrolled the
camera and watched rows 52-92 while the camera moved to base row 49 — so it
never sampled the rows that would have changed.

What settles it in one measurement: dump the array's coverage over a FIXED
ABSOLUTE window, wide enough to contain the camera's whole travel, and look
for cells that are already populated above the camera. On the church map they
are — rows 50-53 hold the building — and scrolling up three tiles draws that
roof from exactly those rows. The data was there; the PPU was not asking.
- **OBJ Y is not clipped.** Games park sprites just off-screen to hide them;
  those will appear in the new rows. The horizontal side answered this with
  `KOL_WS_OBJ_CLIP` and a Y analogue is needed.
- **Affine extrapolates** into margin rows instead of reusing a reference.
  Irrelevant to this game's battle map (mode 0, no affine BG) and unverified
  anywhere else.
- **No scene policy and no disarm.** The "registers held still" property is
  measured for the battle map and one cutscene, not proven for every scene,
  and nothing detects a game that breaks it.

### Units did not appear in the margins — SOLVED 2026-09-21

At any extended width, units standing on the terrain drawn in the left/right
margins were missing; they popped in as the camera reached them.
`states/AO_obj_sides.state` is the repro — at 480x270, tapping left 5 times
brought them in.

**The sprites did not exist.** This was NOT the margin-tilemap situation,
where the guest had already composed the data and the PPU simply was not
asking. Measured over the TCP rig on that state:

```
before      : 21 active, 107 parked, X range -32..226
after 5 left: 30 active,  98 parked, X range -32..219
```

Nine entries move from parked to active and the new ones appear at x = -32,
-16, 0, 16. The active X range never reaches past -32 either way — and that
number is the whole answer.

#### The cull, and it is four immediates

The game has ONE generic sprite emitter, ROM `0x08076810`, and every OBJ goes
through it. It rejects anything outside the GBA's own 240x160 **before**
writing the sprite's fields, so the entry never reaches OAM at all:

```
08076872  8BA8  ldrh  r0,[r5,#0x1C]   ; screen X
08076874  3020  adds  r0,#0x20        ; + left slack          <-- immediate
08076876  0400  lsls  r0,r0,#16       ; truncate to u16
08076878  2198  movs  r1,#0x98        ; limit / 2             <-- immediate
0807687A  0449  lsls  r1,r1,#17       ; 0x98<<17 == 304<<16
0807687C  4288  cmp   r0,r1
0807687E  D818  bhi   0x080768B2      ; REJECT
08076880  201E  movs  r0,#0x1E        ; STRUCT OFFSET, not a bound
08076882  5E29  ldrsh r1,[r5,r0]      ; screen Y
08076884  2010  movs  r0,#0x10        ; top slack             <-- immediate
08076886  4240  rsbs  r0,r0,#0
08076888  4281  cmp   r1,r0
0807688A  DB12  blt   0x080768B2      ; REJECT
0807688C  29C0  cmp   r1,#0xC0        ; bottom limit          <-- immediate
0807688E  DC10  bgt   0x080768B2      ; REJECT
```

Accept window: **X in [-32, 272], Y in [-16, 192]**. The `-32` is exactly the
OAM boundary measured above, which is what confirms this is the right code.

#### The fix: the guest widens its own cull

`game.toml` routes those four immediates — and only those four — through the
framework's opt-in `[[thumb_alu_immediate_override]]` hook, and
`src/kol_obj_cull.{h,cpp}` supplies values derived from the margins actually
being rendered this frame:

```
08076874  left slack     32  + extra_left
08076878  limit / 2      ceil((304 + extra_left + extra_right) / 2)
08076884  top slack      16  + extra_top
0807688C  bottom limit   192 + extra_bottom
```

The immediate reaches the generated code as a plain `uint32_t`, not an 8-bit
field, so none of these is capped at 255 — which matters, because 480 wide
needs a limit of 272 where the original encoding could only hold 255.

This is the whole reason for doing it guest-side rather than synthesising
sprites ourselves: the game emits them, so animation, facing, palette and the
isometric depth sort all still come from the guest.

Gating that matters:
- Zero margins (the authentic 240x160) make the callback decline every site,
  so the generated code keeps its compile-time operand.
- A **pillarboxed** scene also passes zeroes. Its margins are black, so
  widening there would only spend OAM slots on sprites nobody can see.
- `KOL_NO_OBJ_CULL_WIDEN=1` reverts to the stock window at runtime.

Two immediates in the same basic block are deliberately NOT listed:
`0x08076880` is a struct offset used as an `ldrsh` index, and `0x08076890` is
a plain zero.

#### Half two: OAM's X field is 9 bits, and it wraps

Widening the cull fixed the LEFT margin and did nothing for the right, which
is the whole shape of the second bug. OAM's X is a 9-bit field decoded as
